bio.en: Camille Ricketts was the first marketing hire and longtime head of marketing at Notion, previously head of content and marketing at First Round Capital (launching First Round Review) and did comms/PR at early Tesla.
bio.zh: Camille Ricketts 是 Notion 的第一位营销员工和长期营销负责人，此前曾任 First Round Capital 内容与营销负责人（推出 First Round Review），并在早期 Tesla 负责传播与公关。

summary.en: Camille reframes product-market fit through the lens of content-market fit—understanding who your audience is and what they need to avoid failure or gain promotion. She shares lessons from scaling Notion's marketing from near zero and from launching First Round Review, one of the most influential startup publications. The conversation is a practical playbook for content marketing, PR, and building an audience-led growth motion.
summary.zh: Camille 通过“内容市场匹配”的视角重新框定产品市场匹配——理解你的受众是谁、他们有何需求以避免失败或获得晋升。她分享了将 Notion 营销从零做大的经验，以及推出极具影响力的创业出版物 First Round Review 的历程。对话是关于内容营销、公关和打造“受众驱动增长”的实用手册。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: The way that you think about product market fit, you have to think about content market fit. So even though content feels like it's running adjacent to the actual product that you're putting out there, you still have to think about who is my audience? Who is the audience that I really want to have? Who is the audience that is going to be drawn to this most? Who are they? What is it that they really need in their lives? Even abstracting content from it at all. What is it that they need to get promoted? What is it that they need to avoid failure? What is it that causes them a great deal of anxiety in the day-to-day of their lives or their work? And can you create some type of content product that is going to address this for them?
turns.zh: 说到产品市场契合（product market fit），你还得想想内容市场契合（content market fit）。所以尽管内容看起来像是跟你推出去的那款实际产品并行存在的东西，你仍然得想清楚：我的受众是谁？我真正想要的是哪一群受众？哪一群受众最容易被它吸引？他们到底是什么人？他们在生活里真正需要的是什么？哪怕把内容本身完全抽离出来，也想清楚。他们需要在职场上获得晋升，需要避免失败，需要在日常的工作和生活里少一点焦虑——这些又是什么？而你能否做出某种内容产品，去真正解决他们的这些需求？

turns.speaker: Lenny

Camille was the first marketing hire at Notion and longtime head of marketing at Notion. Prior to that, she was head of content and marketing at First Round Capital, where amongst many other things, she launched the First Round Review, which holds a very special place in my heart because a guest post in the First Round Review essentially helped me launch my now career of newsletter and now podcast. Camille also did content marketing at Kiva and also comms and PR at early Tesla where she sat right next to Elon Musk for about a year and she shares some really fun stories about that. (00:01:26): In this episode, we focus on two areas that Camille was very early in and has tremendous insights around. One, community led growth. What it actually is, when it's something you should invest in, how to do it well. All based on her experience building Notion's early community, which was a huge part of Notion's early success. We also talk about content marketing. When it's worth investing in, how to do it well, and all kinds of tips for building a content marketing machine. It was a total blast chatting with Camille and I am really excited for you to learn from her. With that, I bring you Camille Rickets right after we hear a word from our wonderful sponsors. This leads to wasted time building internal tools or trying to run your experiments through a clunky marketing tool. Delivering results quickly, avoiding annoying prolonged analytics cycles, and helping you easily get to the root cause of any issue you discover. Eppo lets you go beyond basic clickthrough metrics, and instead you to North Star metrics like activation, retention, subscriptions and payments. And EPO supports tests on the front end, the back end, email marketing, and even machine learning clients. Check out Eppo, geteppo.com, get E-P-P-O.com and 10X your experiment velocity. Hey, Ashley, head of marketing at Flatfile. How many B2B SaaS companies would you estimate need to import CSV files from their customers?

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.en: At least 40%.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how many of them screw that up and what happens when they do?
turns.zh: 那其中又有多少家会搞砸，搞砸之后又会怎样？

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.en: Well, based on our data, about a third of people will consider switching to another company after just one bad experience during onboarding. So if your CSV importer doesn't work right, which is super common considering customer files are chock full of unexpected data and formatting, they'll leave.
turns.zh: 嗯，根据我们的数据，大概有三分之一的人，只要在 onboarding 阶段有过一次糟糕的体验，就会考虑换一家别的公司。所以如果你的 CSV 导入器不好使——考虑到客户的文件里塞满了各种意料之外的数据和格式，这太常见了——他们就会走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am 0% surprised to hear that. I've consistently seen that improving onboarding is one of the highest leverage opportunities for both signup conversion and increasing long-term retention. Getting people to your aha moment more quickly and reliably is so incredibly important.
turns.zh: 听到这个我一点都不意外。我一贯的观察是，改善 onboarding 是对注册转化和提升长期留存杠杆最高的事情之一。让人更快、更稳地到达那个“啊哈时刻”，实在太重要了。

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.en: Totally. It's incredible to see how our customers like Square, Spotify and Zuora are able to grow their businesses on top of Flatfile. It's because flawless data onboarding acts like a catalyst to get them and their customers where they need to go faster.
turns.zh: 完全同意。看到 Square、Spotify、Zuora 这样的客户能在 Flatfile 之上把业务做大，真的很了不起。原因就在于，无缝的数据 onboarding 就像一个催化剂，能让他们和他们的客户更快到达该去的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you'd like to learn more or get started, check out Flatfile and flatfile.com/lenny. (00:04:27): Camille, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 想了解更多或开始使用，去看看 Flatfile，flatfile.com/lenny。(00:04:27)卡米尔，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Hello there. Thank you so much for having me.
turns.zh: 你好。非常感谢你邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely, my pleasure. You have such a fascinating background working at so many world-class companies with so many fascinating people. Could you just take a minute to talk about some of the wonderful things you've done in your career just to set a little context for folks?
turns.zh: 我的荣幸，很高兴请到你。你的经历太有意思了——在这么多世界级公司、和这么多厉害的人共事过。能不能花一分钟，聊聊你职业生涯里做过的那些精彩的事，先给大家一点背景？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. Well thank you for characterizing them as wonderful.
turns.zh: 嗯，谢谢你用“精彩”来形容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's true.
turns.zh: 真的呀。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I feel like it's been a quite circuitous path, but definitely has taken me to some interesting places. I started off as a journalist at the Wall Street Journal and then found my way into communications and marketing at Tesla Motors where part of my responsibility there was to sit to Elon's right and make sure he had all the data he needed at his fingertips when talking to the press, which was deep end of the pool on the PR learning. And then after that, found my way to First Round Capital where I was really fortunate to be at the ground floor of First Round Review, if anyone out there watching this is familiar with those pieces. Was there for about five years. Loved that team. Really incredible folks. And then they had invested in Notion really early on, and so I was able to meet Ivan Zhao as a result of that and him and Simon, and they gave me the opportunity to join as the first marketing hire at Notion. And that's what I was doing up until recently.
turns.zh: 我觉得自己的职业路径挺绕的，但确实把我带到了一些很有意思的地方。我一开始是《华尔街日报》的记者，后来转到特斯拉汽车做传播和市场，当时我的职责之一，就是坐在埃隆右边，确保他在跟媒体交谈时，手边随时有他需要的所有数据——那在公关学习上算是直接跳进了深水区。再之后，我去了 First Round Capital，很幸运能参与 First Round Review 从零起步的过程，看这期节目的朋友如果熟悉那些文章应该知道。我在那儿待了大概五年，特别喜欢那个团队，一群真的很强的人。后来他们很早就投资了 Notion，也正是因为这个机缘，我认识了 Ivan Zhao，还有他和 Simon，他们给了我机会，让我以第一位市场 hires 的身份加入 Notion。直到前不久，我做的都是这件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that Elon tidbit. I like that it was on his right. His right hand person. What was that like? And is there something that you learned working alongside Elon, sitting next to Elon, about operating, working that maybe you've taken to other places you worked at?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢埃隆这个小细节了。我喜欢那是坐在他右边——他右手边的人。那是什么感觉？还有，在埃隆身边、坐在他旁边工作，你有没有学到什么关于运营、关于做事的东西，后来带到了你工作过的其他地方？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I mean, it was a long time ago, so I'll caveat that. This was before Model S came out even. So a lot of my work was, and this was a great opportunity, but driving around in the Roadster and talking to journalists and letting reporters ride in the car, which was very seductive and I think maybe just a little unfair from a PR standpoint. But in terms of what I learned, that was really the first job that I had that was necessitating just being incredibly on point with all the information. So making sure that I knew everything that could possibly come up in a conversation, being incredibly well-versed in just the topics at hand, I think that served me really well. I just have to be really, really, really quick and on it. And then the other thing that Elon I think is very talented at or definitely at the time really made an impression on me was painting an emotional picture of the vision that he was really going after and being able to convey the emotional quality of the mission to the people he talked to. So definitely at the time about the electric vehicle revolution and then space travel, I think he just knew how to make people feel about it that really enlisted a lot of hearts and minds and that is something that I've taken with me for sure.
turns.zh: 嗯，那已经是挺久以前的事了，所以我先打个预防针。那甚至还是在 Model S 出来之前。所以我的很多工作——虽然是个很棒的机会——就是开着 Roadster 到处跑，跟记者聊天，让记者坐进车里体验，这招特别有诱惑力，不过从公关角度看，我猜可能有点不太公平。但说到我学到的东西，那真的是我第一份逼着我对所有信息都极度精准到位的工作。也就是说，要确保自己清楚一场对话里可能冒出来的任何事，对当下这些话题烂熟于心，我觉得这让我受益良多。我必须真的、真的、真的反应快、跟得上。还有另一点，我觉得埃隆非常擅长、至少在那个时候确实让我印象深刻的，就是把他真正在追求的那个愿景描绘成一幅有画面感的、带着情绪的图景，并且能把这项使命的情感分量传达给跟他交谈的人。当时说的当然是电动车革命，后来还有太空旅行——我觉得他就是懂得怎么让人对这件事产生共鸣，从而真正打动很多人的心和脑，这一点我肯定一直带在身上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Would you say that was the most stressful place you've worked or have you found more stress post Elon?
turns.zh: 你会说那是你工作过压力最大的地方吗，还是在离开埃隆之后，你遇到了更大的压力？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I think that that was the place where you just needed to be so on your game. Game face every single day. Which is a wonderful skill to learn. And then I think there were other moments in my career where just the stakes might have been a little bit higher. Certainly at Notion every day felt like we're building this thing together and we're in this very special moment. So yeah, I think there was a mix there.
turns.zh: 我觉得在那一，你得每天都保持最佳状态，每天都得戴着那张“职业面孔”。这倒是门很值得学的本事。然后我职业生涯里也有一些别的时刻，赌注可能还更高一点。当然，在 Notion 的时候，每天的感觉都像是我们在一起打造这件东西，正处在一个非常特别的时刻。所以，我觉得两方面都有吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of Notion, I think you mentioned this and if not, you were the first marketing hire at Notion. Is that right?
turns.zh: 说到 Notion，我记得你提过，就算没提过——你是 Notion 的第一位市场 hires，对吧？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What employee number was that?
turns.zh: 那是第几号员工？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I was number 11.
turns.zh: 我是第 11 号员工。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. So it was really a small squad of folks at the time.
turns.zh: 嗯，所以当时真的是一小拨人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how big are they now, roughly would you say?
turns.zh: 那他们现在大概多大了，你觉得？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: The last I heard, I think that they were around 400. Maybe a little over 400.
turns.zh: 我最近听到的消息，好像是在 400 人左右，可能稍微多一点，超过 400。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And I think they're worth ... I don't know. Last valuation was like $10 billion. So there's been quite the journey. Must have been quite the adventure being at Notion during this time. What's maybe the most tangible memory of working at Notion in the early days? What was it like early day Notion?
turns.zh: 太厉害了。估值嘛……我不太清楚，上次估值好像是 100 亿美元左右。这一路走下来真不容易。能在 Notion 这段时期待着，肯定是一场大冒险。在 Notion 早期工作，最具体的记忆是什么？早期 Notion 到底是什么样？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I think a lot about just what the environment felt like. This was the first very small startup that I had worked for. When I left First Round, I really wanted that experience. And the first office that I worked in was really just like a home. It literally had an apartment on top of this loft space and it just felt like we were a group of people who lived there together during the day, but it had that kind of home spun really warm quality. So we all took our shoes off. There was beautiful furnishings and rugs and we would all just sit around and drink tea and work together on these couches. So it really had that feeling to it. And then there were little quirks. I like to reminisce with my colleagues who were there at the time that we didn't have a great HVAC system. (00:08:58): So during the summer it was really hot and then in the winter it was really cold and we would have these big industrial fans and at the time we were like, "Oh, this is really bizarre." But now it's one of our favorite memories to talk about. Or for a while we didn't have overhead lighting, so me and my colleagues who were there working really late at night, it would just get darker and darker and darker. And one of my favorite folks there actually had a headlamp that she would switch on at a certain point in the evening. So that's the stuff that really comes up for me. We were all working really hard and in this thing together, but it's that team familial quality that stands out to me.
turns.zh: 我经常会想起那种环境的感觉。那是我工作过的第一家很小的初创公司。我离开 First Round 的时候，真的特别想要那种体验。我工作的第一个办公室，真的就像个家。它在这个 loft 空间的顶上，真的有一套公寓，给人的感觉就像我们这群人白天一起住在那儿，但它又有那种自家手工打造的、很温暖的特质。所以我们都脱了鞋。那里有漂亮的家具和地毯，我们就都围着沙发坐着、喝着茶、一起工作。所以它真的有那种氛围。然后还有一些小怪癖。我喜欢跟当时在场的同事一起回味，我们那套 HVAC（空调通风）系统不怎么样。(00:08:58)所以夏天特别热，冬天又特别冷，我们就摆着那些大工业风扇，当时我们还说“噢，这也太离谱了”。但现在这反倒成了我们最爱聊的回忆之一。还有一阵子我们没有顶灯，所以我和那些同事半夜还在加班的时候，屋子就越来越暗、越来越暗。当时有个我很喜欢的人，她会在晚上某个点戴上头灯。这些就是最先浮现在我脑海里的画面。我们当时都特别拼命，一起在做这件事，但让我印象最深的，是那种家人般的团队气质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how some of these early moments where it feels like, what the hell are we doing? We have to wear headlamps? It's super hot. When you're in it, you're like, this isn't maybe how our startup should be going. And it feels really painful and hard. But looking back, it's always the best memories, those hardships.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢早期那些时刻——你会觉得，我们到底在干什么？还得戴头灯？热得要死。身在其中时你会想，我们的创业不该是这么个走法吧。当时又痛又难。但回头看，那些苦日子永远是最好的回忆。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: It truly is. And the moments that we were there late at night really trying to get something done before a big launch the next day, that's where our hearts lie, I think, to a large extent. That crew that was there.
turns.zh: 真的是。那些深夜我们还守在那儿、为了第二天的大发布拼命想把事情赶完的时刻，很大程度上，我们的心就系在那里。就在那群人中间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that note, and when you're talking about stress working with Elon, you talked about Notion had a different kind of stress. What's maybe the most stressful memory you have of working at Notion? Whatever you can share.
turns.zh: 顺着这个说，你刚聊到跟埃隆共事的压力，又说 Notion 是另一种压力。那你在 Notion 工作，最有压力的记忆是什么？能分享的都可以说。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: This is something that has long since been rectified, but the first day that we came back from break in 2021 ... We had all been sort of away for the holidays. We reassemble. I think it's January 3rd, 2021 perhaps. Had a massive outage that day that took down, not just us but also a lot of our peer companies. And so it was literally all hands on deck. We're suddenly seeing all of these people on Twitter pop up, on the Reddit pop up being like, "Oh my gosh. What am I going to do?" And it really reinforced for us how central Notion had become to so many people. So on one hand it was kind of this amazing moment of realization of how vital this thing we were building was all the time, which adds to the stress in the moment, but also your motivation overall. (00:11:01): And then we also saw on Twitter, and this is part of why community is such a core focus of mine, but people being like, "They're trying really hard to get it back up. Give them a break." Or like, "Sending hugs to the Notion team. We know you've got this." And we really appreciated that and that was just a very heartwarming aspect of it. But that day was definitely a scramble and we wanted to be as communicative as possible. So my team was really central to making sure that everybody knew what was going on, what the efforts were being made to fix it, time horizon, all of that. So they've long since hired the best infrastructure people I think in the industry and refactored the database and everything. So it's not an issue anymore, but certainly that was a moment of stress at the time.
turns.zh: 这事早就解决了，但 2021 年我们假期结束回来的第一天……大家节后回来，重新聚到一起。我记得大概是 2021 年 1 月 3 日。那天发生了一场大宕机，不光是我们，很多同行公司也一起挂了。所以真的是全员上阵。我们突然看到 Twitter、Reddit 上冒出来一堆人，说什么“天哪，我该怎么办？”这也让我们真切体会到，Notion 对那么多人来说已经变得多中心化。所以一方面，这是个挺惊人的时刻，让你意识到我们一直在打造的东西有多不可或缺——这既加重了当下的压力，也加重了你整体的动力。(00:11:01)然后我们在 Twitter 上也看到——这也是为什么社区对我来说这么核心——有人会说“他们真的很努力在恢复了，给他们点空间吧”，或者“给 Notion 团队送个抱抱，我们知道你们可以的”。我们真的特别感激，那是很暖心的一面。但那天绝对是一场手忙脚乱，我们想尽可能地把信息同步出去。所以我的团队非常关键，要确保每个人都知道发生了什么、我们在怎么修、大概要多久，所有这些。后来他们早就招到了我觉得业内最顶尖的基础设施人才，重构了数据库，一切都搞定了。所以现在不是问题了，但当时那确实是个压力时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting looking at those times. When you're in it, you're like, "We are going to die. We're down. People will stop using Notion. We're in big trouble." When really people always come back if it's an awesome product. I think of last things down for a week, JIRA or Confluent, and people come back if it's an awesome product.
turns.zh: 回看那些时候挺有意思。身在其中你会想“我们要完蛋了，挂了，大家会不用 Notion 了，我们麻烦大了”。但其实只要产品够好，人们总会回来的。我想到 JIRA、Confluent 那些宕机整整一周的例子，只要产品够好，人们就会回来。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I think that's a good tactical learning and hopefully a takeaway for folks who maybe will experience that moment is that truly there's more resilience built into the system than you might think.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是个很好的战术性经验，也希望那些可能会遇到这种时刻的人能记住一点：系统里其实内置了比你想象中更强的韧性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So speaking of community, you talked about just how important that was during this time and then just in general. I was doing research on you and things that you've done over your career to prep for this podcast and I found there's two areas that you've led the charge on and we're ahead of the curve on and in part help innovate. One is community led growth and two is content marketing in a big way. And so I wanted to focus a lot of our chat on these two areas. Community led growth, it feels like a very buzzy topic on Twitter. Everyone's always talking about how the future of growth is community. You've got to build a community. You got to be community led and all these things. And so I want to try to make this concept concrete and help people understand should they invest in community. How can community help you? When does it make sense to you? When does it not make sense to invest? And so maybe just as a first question, just what is community led growth? What does that actually mean as a concept?
turns.zh: 说到社区，你刚说这段时间它有多重要，而且总体上一直都重要。我在为这期播客做准备时，做了点关于你的研究，发现有两个领域是你带头做的、而且走在了前面、某种程度上还推动了创新。一个是社区驱动增长，二是内容营销，而且是大规模的内容营销。所以我想把咱们大部分对话聚焦在这两个领域上。社区驱动增长，在 Twitter 上感觉是个特别火的词，所有人都在说增长的未来是社区，你得建社区，你得靠社区驱动，诸如此类。所以我想把这个概念讲具体，帮大家想清楚到底该不该投社区。社区能怎么帮你？什么时候对你有意义？什么时候投进去没意义？所以作为第一个问题，社区驱动增长到底是什么？这个概念到底指什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. I think it has become quite buzzy and it's certainly aspirational for a lot of product led growth companies and even those that are maybe a little bit outside of the product led growth orbit. And we're seeing all of these startups I think also come out that are about community and how to enhance the effects. In terms of how I think about what it actually is, it's when your community helps you achieve such ubiquity and such name recognition that it actually allows you to start moving upmarket into the enterprise. And I know that might be very specific to enterprise oriented companies, but that's how we defined it at Notion was the fact that so many people were talking about this, sharing what they had built about it, honestly starting businesses of their own around it to formalize the relationship with teams that I think it de-risked Notion as a choice for a lot of companies just because they had heard about it through so many channels. They had seen it on social media, they've heard about it on a podcast, their friend told them about it, they saw a billboard. All of that lended itself to larger and larger companies and teams buying more and more seats. So I think that's the power that the community had for us. And I see that also being analogous to what companies like Figma have been able to achieve.
turns.zh: 嗯。我觉得它确实变得很火，而且对很多产品驱动增长（PLG）的公司、甚至那些可能稍微在 PLG 圈子之外一点的公司来说，都很有吸引力。我们也看到一堆关于社区、关于怎么放大社区效应的初创公司冒出来。至于我怎么理解它到底是什么——就是当你的社区帮你做到了足够的渗透和知名度，以至于它真的能让你开始往上游走、打企业市场。我知道这可能对企业导向的公司特别具体，但我们在 Notion 就是这么定义的：有那么多人在聊它、分享自己用它能搭出什么、甚至真的围绕它开起了自己的公司，把和团队的关系正式化——我认为这很大程度上帮很多公司消除了选择 Notion 的风险，因为他们从太多渠道都听说过它。他们在社交媒体上看到过，在播客里听过，朋友告诉过他们，还看到过广告牌。所有这些，让越来越大、越来越大的公司和团队买下越来越多的席位。所以我觉得，这就是社区对我们的力量。我也看到 Figma 这类公司实现了类似的效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds like a lot of the way you're describing it is basically awareness. Brand awareness is what you found to be maybe the most useful element of this community that you built around Notion.
turns.zh: 听起来你说的很多，本质上就是认知度。品牌认知度，是你觉得围绕 Notion 建的这个社区最有用的部分？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I love using the word discovery because I think that that is even a little bit like a step further than awareness where true discovery is when you have intent to find out more. You've heard about it so many times or you've been intrigued by something that someone has told you to the extent that you're actually going to take the step of now learning about it. And that's where we really wanted to play and to emphasize our work.
turns.zh: 我更喜欢用“发现”（discovery）这个词，因为我觉得它比认知度还往前走了一步——真正的发现，是你有了去了解更多一下的意图。你听过它太多次，或者被别人说的某件事勾起了兴趣，以至于你真的会迈出去了解它的那一步。那才是我们真正想发力、想重点强调的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So it sounded like the KPI/OKR of your team was get more people aware and excited to explore Notion.
turns.zh: 明白了。这么听来，你们团队的 KPI/OKR 就是让更多人知道 Notion、并且兴奋地想去探索它。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. And maybe this is a helpful tactical point. I think when people think about acquisition or discovery or brand awareness or brand in general, they're like what collection of metrics are actually going to give us insight into this? And the one that I found to be the most instructive was net new visitors to the Notion website. So month over month, how many new people who had never been there before were motivated enough to come and actually learn about the product. And that was really the responsibility of the brand team and the folks that worked with me on community and content and all of the awareness campaigns that we were putting out into the field was about getting more new people interested.
turns.zh: 对。这也许是个有用的战术点。我觉得当人们想到获客、发现、品牌认知或者品牌整体时，会问：到底哪一组指标能真正给我们这方面的洞察？而我发现最有指导意义的，是 Notion 官网的净新增访客。也就是按月看，有多少从没来过的人，被激发到足够有动力真正点进来、去了解这个产品。而那真的就是品牌团队、还有跟我一起做社区和内容、以及我们投放到市场上的所有认知度活动的同事的责任——就是要让更多新人对它产生兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So that begs to the question, did you have any clever ways of attributing that new traffic to stuff your team did versus the SEO team or other teams?
turns.zh: 这就引出一个问题：你有没有什么聪明的办法，把那些新增流量归因到你们团队做的事上，而不是归到 SEO 团队或者其他团队头上？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: In particular I'll call out the influencer marketing efforts that were really being run by this incredible woman, Lexi Barnhorn, where they were incredibly measurable. Where we were like, okay, well we're sponsoring people for this amount, these creators across these platforms and we know that people came from that content directly to the Notion website. So we were able to draw really tight connections. So I think that some types of content lend themselves to that. And then also with community, there's certain things you can do around helping your community members report on how many people are attending, et cetera, to give you that sense.
turns.zh: 特别要提一下红人营销那块，那主要是由一个特别厉害的姑娘 Lexi Barnhorn 在操盘，而且可量化程度非常高。我们当时就想，好，我们花这么多钱赞助这些人、这些在各个平台上的创作者，而且我们知道确实有人是从那些内容直接跳到了 Notion 官网。所以我们能建立起非常紧密的关联。我觉得有些类型的内容天然就适合这种归因。另外在社区的层面，你也可以做一些事，比如帮你的社区成员汇报有多少人在参与等等，从而让你有那种感觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you may be already answering this question, but I'm curious what efforts had the most impact to achieve these goals that you had of creating more awareness and discovery motivation and things like that. What actually worked?
turns.zh: 你可能已经在回答这个问题了，但我还是好奇：在达成你那些目标——创造更多认知、激发发现产品的动力等等——的过程中，哪些动作影响最大？到底什么真的管用？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: So I'd say that the community efforts that were very big for us we're the ambassadors. Also making sure that people were hosting in-person events. This really took off in 2019. Obviously we paused for 2020, 2021, but now I just spent time with Notion's head of community, Ben Lang, who truly is the mastermind and genius behind so much of this and he says that they're back up to 30 in-person events a month around the world. So that really helped on the international scale of spreading ubiquity and ended up lending itself to relationships with Station F in France, which is the biggest startup campus in Paris. So really helping us work our way into those types of networks and then supporting those people to also start their own businesses and derive whatever reward they were looking for themselves. So we really wanted to align our goals with theirs. (00:17:38): A lot of those folks actually started revenue generating businesses as consultants or course makers or influencers. Some of them just wanted to build their own platforms online. So all of our efforts there are around building guides or counseling people one-on-one or making it easier for them to actually achieve those goals for themselves was also a big part of this growth. And then like I said, influencers. This was something that Ben started exploring in 2019 and we were so pleasantly overwhelmed with the amount of traction and traffic that was driven by working with some of these influencers. And now that program has exploded into a multi-channel effort that's huge for Notion.
turns.zh: 我会说，对我们帮助最大的社区动作，是那些大使（ambassadors），还有确保大家都在办线下活动。这在 2019 年真的起飞了。当然 2020、2021 我们停了，但我刚跟 Notion 的社区负责人 Ben Lang 聊过，他真的是这方面很多事的操盘手和天才，他说现在全球每个月又回到了 30 场线下活动。所以这在把知名度铺向国际层面真的帮了大忙，最后也促成了我们和法国 Station F（巴黎最大的创业园区）的关系。所以确实帮我们打进了那类网络，然后又去支持那些人，让他们也能开起自己的公司、得到他们自己想要的回报。所以我们真的很想让他们的目标和我们的目标对齐。(00:17:38)那些人里，很多真的做起了能赚钱的生意——做顾问、做课程、做红人。有些人只是想在网上建自己的平台。所以我们在那块的所有动作，不管是写指南、一对一辅导，还是让他们更容易去实现自己的那些目标，也都是这个增长里很大的一块。然后就像我说的，红人。这是 Ben 在 2019 年开始探索的，而那些红人带来的流量和势头，量大到让我们又惊喜又有点招架不住。现在那个项目已经炸开，变成了一个多渠道、对 Notion 极其重要的动作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. The influencers makes a lot of sense. I want to learn more about this ambassador program and what that was about with events and maybe just broadly, I imagine a lot of founders might be listening and they're like, "Yeah, this all sounds awesome, but how do you know if it's doing anything?" Events. That would be great, but how much is it worth investing? How much time and attention does it take? How do we know if this is actually ROI positive? Is there anything you learn there about just ... Is it a founder must believe in this as a thing that is probably going to work sort of thing? Or is there something you found to convince people like, yes, this is how you can know it's working?
turns.zh: 太棒了。红人那块很有道理。我想多了解这个大使计划，还有它跟活动是什么关系。更宽泛地说，我猜很多创始人听着会觉得“嗯，这些都听起来很棒，但你怎么知道它到底有没有用？”活动，听起来不错，但值得投多少？要花多少时间和精力？我们怎么知道它真的 ROI 为正？你在这方面有没有学到什么——是说创始人必须先相信这东西大概率会管用呢，还是说你找到了什么办法去说服人：“对，这样你就能知道它在起作用了”？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: That's a great question. I think that we were really fortunate that Ivan saw the inherent value in community from the very beginning and was deeply supportive. And actually one of my number one recommendations for anybody who suspects the community could be a big growth driver is to not make metrics the be all end all at the very beginning. So we didn't necessarily start measuring things very concretely until last year with community. Mostly because we had already seen so much organic scale that we saw being tied to our community efforts in some way in terms of where we were geographically expanding, how people were reporting that they had discovered us whenever we surveyed them. So that type of motion. And I think for any company that is seeing this type of just organic fervor, one of the worst things you can do is say, let's cut this off at the knees if it's not generating ROI.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。我觉得我们真的很幸运，Ivan 从一开始就看到了社区的内在价值，而且非常支持。其实我对任何怀疑社区可能是个大增长引擎的人，头号建议就是：在最开始，别把指标当成唯一标准。所以我们对社区的衡量，其实直到去年才真正具体起来。主要因为我们早就看到了那么多自发的规模，而且从我们地理上扩张到哪里、人们在调研里怎么说发现我们的，都能某种程度上跟社区动作挂钩。就是这种态势。而我觉得，对任何正在经历这种自发热情的公司来说，最糟糕的做法之一就是：如果它一时没产生 ROI，就说“砍了吧”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine internally there's just like obviously this is good. We may not be able to measure it, but it feels like this is very good for Notion. It feels like especially for a prosumer product like Notion, it makes a lot of sense because it's driven by people using it and then they bring it into the company, like you said. Maybe it's less ROI positive or just one enterprise product. Do you have any thoughts there? Is this a great strategy for prosumer enterprise products more so than more enterprise-y?
turns.zh: 我猜在内部，大家就是觉得“这显然是好事。我们也许没法量化，但感觉这对 Notion 特别好”。尤其对 Notion 这种 prosumer（专业消费者）产品，这特别说得通，因为它是靠人们自己用起来、再把它带进公司，就像你说的。也许对单一的企业级产品，ROI 就没那么正。你在这方面怎么看？比起更偏企业级的产品，这是不是对 prosumer 类的企业产品更有效的策略？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Definitely I think if you have a long sales cycle or a high price point where there has to be many, many, many touchpoints in order to get somebody to decide to buy, I'm not sure that community should be the number one thing that you invest in. Certainly for freemium products, I think for a lot of them, especially if they have what I'm going to call the atomic unit of sharing, which I will define out, it becomes a no-brainer. I think that community lends itself particularly well if you have something that your product creates that people want to share because it exhibits something about themselves. So at Notion it was templates or even people just creating their own workspaces and being really excited to show them off. So Notion really benefited from being a creative product, but the same is true of Figma or Canva or any of these where showing people what it is that you've created is an aspirational thing to do. Because you are showing that you are really well versed in how to use the products, extremely organized. You're self expressing in some way. So if your product does have that element to it, I think that community is a great investment.
turns.zh: 绝对。我觉得如果你有很长的销售周期，或者很高的客单价，需要很多很多很多次触达才能让一个人决定购买，我不确定社区该是你投入的第一优先级。当然对免费增值（freemium）产品，我觉得对其中很多——尤其是如果有那种我称之为“分享的最小单元”（atomic unit of sharing）的东西，我待会儿定义——那就是理所当然该做的。我觉得，如果你的产品能创造出让人们想分享、因为它能展示自己某一方面东西的时候，社区就特别合适。在 Notion，那就是模板，甚至只是人们搭出自己的 workspace、特别兴奋地想炫耀。所以 Notion 确实受益于它是一个有创造力的产品，但 Figma、Canva 或者任何这类产品也一样——把你自己做的东西秀给别人看，本身就是一件有向往感的事。因为你在展示你对这个产品用得多溜、多有条理，你在某种程度上做自我表达。所以如果你的产品有这个元素，我觉得社区就是一笔很值得的投资。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on this point, and I don't think people realize this, but you can make a lot of money creating templates on Notion, right? That's a whole ecosystem. Can you talk about that? Because I don't think a lot of people know this.
turns.zh: 你提到了这一点，但我觉得大家没意识到——在 Notion 上做模板是可以赚很多钱的，对吧？那是一个完整的生态。你能聊聊这个吗？因为我觉得很多人不知道。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. This is one of the reasons that I would advise any of the companies that feel like they fall into this category start early. Because you need to nurture all of these different routes that people in your community can take. Certainly early on I think that the people that we initially recruited in the ambassadors didn't see themselves doing maybe even close to a million dollars in business around helping other teams succeed with the product or selling templates. I remember really early on, probably mid 2021 we heard of one creator who had made $35,000 in four months selling one template and that was a very common story then from that point forward. And helping them do that, actually creating the guide material and the networks and also the connections between the people who are running similar businesses who could help each other, that all became really fundamental. But to your point about, oh is this actually related to the enterprise motion for Notion? So many companies now of many sizes are relying on the consultants that first came up through our community and some of those consultants are now employing dozens of other people.
turns.zh: 对。这也是我建议任何觉得自己属于这类公司的，要尽早开始的原因之一。因为你需要去培育社区里人们能走的所有这些不同路径。当然早期，我觉得我们最初招募的那些大使，可能都没想到自己能围绕“帮别的团队用好这个产品”或者“卖模板”做出接近一百万美元的生意。我记得很早的时候，大概是 2021 年中，我们听说一个创作者在四个月里靠卖一个模板赚了 3.5 万美元，而从那以后这就成了很常见的故事。而帮他们做到这一点——真的去写指南素材、建网络、还把做类似生意、能互相帮助的人连起来——这些都变得非常基础。但说到你那个点，哦，这跟 Notion 的企业级打法到底有没有关系？现在好多不同规模的公司，都在依赖那些最早从我们社区里成长起来的顾问，其中一些顾问现在手底下雇着几十号人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. There's no better way to motivate someone to evangelize Notion than have their income rely on Notion.
turns.zh: 太了不起了。没有什么比让一个人的收入依赖 Notion，更能激励他去传播 Notion 了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: And it's also just inspiring for us, honestly. There's so many people who started off with not very many followers and now they are celebrities within this ecosystem.
turns.zh: 而且说实话，对我们来说这也挺鼓舞人的。太多人一开始没多少粉丝，现在已经是这个生态里的名人了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So maybe coming back to the ambassador program, that's separate from this selling Notion templates ecosystem. What is the ambassador program?
turns.zh: 那回到大使计划——它是跟“卖 Notion 模板”那个生态分开的，对吧？大使计划到底是什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: They're actually quite blended because the folks who are excited about Notion, it takes a lot of forms. Sometimes they want to host events, sometimes they want to build templates. So we would actually have channels inside of our Slack instance for the ambassadors that had these areas of focus based on what people really were passionate about or wanted to do and they were like a force multiplying flywheel for each other. Because a lot of folks would enter the ambassadors program and then I'm happy to talk about champions as well, which is a little bit different, and then discover what it would mean for them to build templates and it became motivating for that reason. So on the champions side of things, and this is maybe speaking a little bit more to the enterprise as well, we wondered if the same DNA that existed among consumers for the most part in the ambassadors could work for folks who were inside of our customer companies. And so we launched another community, another Slack instance for folks who were the most passionate or the most avid users of Notion inside of our customer companies, which has become just a wonderful channel for customer success to be more communicative with those companies, make sure that things are sticking or obstacles are being overcome. And that's been designed very specifically that way and it has been really, really valuable over time.
turns.zh: 其实这两块融合得挺深的，因为那些对 Notion 兴奋的人，表现形式很多样。有时他们想办活动，有时想做模板。所以我们其实在大使们的 Slack 里，按大家真正有热情或想做的事，分了不同的频道，而他们彼此之间形成了一个放大彼此的飞轮。因为很多人进了大使计划——我也很乐意聊聊 champions（略有不同的一类）——然后才发现“原来做模板对我意味着什么”，并因此被激发了动力。所以在 champions 那一侧，这也多少跟企业级更相关一点：我们当时在想，大使里那种主要存在于消费者身上的 DNA，能不能也用在客户公司里的人身上。于是我们又建了另一个社区、另一个 Slack 实例，专门给那些在我们客户公司里最热情、最铁杆的用户，这后来成了客户成功去跟那些公司更畅通沟通的一个特别棒的渠道——确保大家用得顺、障碍被扫清。而且这从设计上就是这么明确的，久而久之真的非常有价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So let me try to understand this. Champions are basically the most active users of Notion. You put them in a Slack and help them become even more excited and make sure they're happy. Ambassador. I still don't totally understand what is an ambassador? Is that someone you're paying to help promote Notion? What does that actually mean when you're an ambassador?
turns.zh: 好，那我试着理解一下。Champions 基本就是 Notion 最活跃的用户。你把他们放进一个 Slack，帮他们更兴奋、确保他们开心。那大使呢？我还是没完全搞懂大使到底是什么？是你付钱让他帮忙推广 Notion 的人吗？当你是大使的时候，这到底意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: They're people who are really just passionate about the product. So it's not transactional. They're people who love building with Notion. They love sharing what they've built in order to help others. And they really just want it to be a bigger part of their lives. And I think that one of the points about community is that it's not just a one-to-one conversation with us. The big draw over time, maybe people joined because they would get early access to features. We would get their feedback. That became really important for our product team or because we would offer AMAs with some of our folks internally. But over time it was really because they were forming these bonds with each other and learning so much from each other that most of the time someone would come in and say, I'm struggling with this or I don't quite know how to use this and it would be another member of the community that would help them more immediately. So it really allowed them to form these dense networks of friendships that I think became just a positive part of people's lives.
turns.zh: 他们就是真心热爱这个产品的人。所以这不是交易关系。他们是热爱用 Notion 搭建东西的人，热爱分享自己搭的东西去帮别人。他们就是想让 Notion 在自己生活里占更大的比重。而我觉得关于社区有一点：它不只是在跟我们做一对一的对话。随着时间，吸引人的地方或许是大家因为能抢先体验功能而加入，我们会收集他们的反馈——这对我们的产品团队变得非常重要——或者因为我们提供过跟内部同事的 AMA。但久而久之，真正的原因其实是他们彼此之间建立了联结，从彼此身上学到很多，大多数时候，有人进来问“我这个卡住了”或者“我不太会用这个”，往往是另一个社区成员更及时地帮了他们。所以这真的让他们形成了那种紧密的友谊网络，我觉得那成了人们生活中很正向的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm taking away from this partly is you identify a group of people that are interested in Notion, excited about Notion and then just lean in to support them. There's people that are buying Notion and that are power users, help them be better power users. Influencers that are kind of excited about Notion, pay them to promote Notion. Then the ambassadors that are people just passionate about Notion, help them be more passionate. And then the people making templates, help them be successful. Is that roughly how you think about it? Just identify something that's working and make it more effective?
turns.zh: 我从中得到的一点体会是：你先识别出一群对 Notion 感兴趣、为 Notion 兴奋的人，然后就倾身去支持他们。有人在买 Notion、是重度用户，就帮他们成为更好的重度用户；对 Notion 有点兴奋的红人，付钱让他们推广 Notion；然后大使是那些单纯热爱 Notion 的人，就帮他们更热爱；再做模板的人，就帮他们成功。大概你就是这么想的？就是识别出哪些事在起作用，然后让它更高效？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I think if it doesn't sound too reductive, yes. I would also say that one of the things that I think Ben was best at is not putting a one size fits all experience on any of this. I think that some communities get built where people are like, okay, well we have this community and it's going to be this and this and this, or these are the types of programs we're going to offer or these are the types of interactions we're going to have. As opposed to I think a lot of listening of the people who are actually participating. Really early on one of the things that Ben did that I thought was really amazing was he'd spend a ton of time just on Zoom having conversations, one-on-one conversations, semi small group conversations just saying, "Why are you here? Why do you like participating in this? What is it that would make it better?" And really helping our entire team follow their lead. I would recommend highly not necessarily coming in with preconceived notions about what a community needs to look like.
turns.zh: 如果听起来不太简化，是的。我还想说，我觉得 Ben 最擅长的一点，就是不给任何一块套上一个“一刀切”的体验。我觉得有些社区建起来时，人们会想“好，我们有这个社区了，它就该是这样这样这样”，或者“我们要提供的是这几类项目”“我们要的是这几类互动”。而不是去大量倾听真正在参与的人。很早的时候，Ben 做了一件我觉得特别厉害的事：他会花大量时间，就泡在 Zoom 上，做一对一、或半小型组的对话，就问“你为什么在这儿？你为什么喜欢参与这个？什么能让它变得更好？”然后真的帮我们整个团队跟着他们的节奏走。我强烈建议，不要带着对社区“应该长什么样”的先入为主的想法进来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on this, that if the founder believes in the power of community, this becomes so much easier. A lot of founders are like, "Nah. That's a waste of time." Do you think founders are convincible that building community and investing in community is worth it? Have you seen that effective where a founder just comes into it being like, "Nah, I don't think this is worth our time," and then they get convinced later? Or is it just like, "Nah, forget it. Don't even try."?
turns.zh: 你提到过，如果创始人相信社区的力量，这事就简单太多了。很多创始人会想“算了，那是浪费时间”。你觉得创始人能被说服、相信建社区、投社区是值得的吗？你有没有见过这种真的奏效的情况：一个创始人一开始“不，我觉得这不值得花时间”，后来被说服了？还是说往往就是“算了吧，别试了”？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I mean I've talked to a lot of different people who come at this with different impressions and everybody knows more about their company than I do, but I do think that if ubiquity or just the sheer word of mouth engine is something that is going to be valuable for your company over time, I would really urge people to sit down and really think carefully what is going to be more conducive to our long-term success? Is it going to be that ubiquity or is it going to be revenue now? And I think if we look at a lot of the companies that have been just wildly successful from the start, they're people who have pushed off maybe monetizing every little thing if it's going to really put a damper on that type of enthusiasm and momentum that people have to share it at what it is they're doing. Because there's always opportunity I think later once you have that big tide of people who are not just excited but also legitimizing what it is that you do every single day, that gets mobilized in a lot of different directions and you have a lot more options then.
turns.zh: 我聊过很多持不同看法的人，而且每个人都比我自己更了解他们的公司。但我确实觉得，如果“铺开知名度”或者说那种纯粹的口碑引擎，长期来说对你的公司是有价值的，我会真的劝大家坐下来认真想想：什么才更利于我们的长期成功？是那种知名度，还是眼下的收入？我觉得如果看很多一开始就特别成功的公司，它们都是愿意推迟去把每一样东西都变现的人——如果变现会真的打击人们去分享“自己在做什么”的那股热情和势头的话。因为我觉得，一旦你有了那股大潮——人们不仅兴奋，而且每天都在为你做的事背书、赋予它正当性——它就会被调动到很多不同的方向，到那时你的选择就多得多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting about Notion is you have high LTVs when you sell to larger companies, but the initial users are often just regular folks. And so I think it's a unique place where you have cash to spend on making it ubiquitous and getting the word out through all these community efforts because it'll pay off. And a lot of companies probably don't have that advantage. So would it feel right to say that this is really effective for product led, growthy, freemium products most? Is that a good way to think about it?
turns.zh: Notion 有意思的一点是，你卖给大公司时 LTV（客户终身价值）很高，但最初的用户往往就是普通人。所以我觉得它处在一个独特的位置：你有现金去花在“让它无处不在”、通过所有这些社区动作把声音传出去上，因为最后会回本。而很多公司可能没这个优势。所以这么说对吗——这招对产品驱动、增长型、免费增值产品最有效？这么想算对路吗？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. Or I think if organic growth is something that you see being really beneficial or if organic growth happens to be something you really have to crack because you don't always have everything you need for paid growth from either a resourcing standpoint, team standpoint, really figuring out how to get that organic flywheel going can serve you well. It becomes this buttress for any paid growth you explore in the future.
turns.zh: 对。或者我觉得，如果自然增长是你看到确实很有好处的东西，或者你不得不去啃下自然增长——因为你在付费增长上不一定总是具备所需的资源、团队条件——那真正搞清楚怎么让那个自然增长的飞轮转起来，对你很有帮助。它会成为你未来任何付费增长探索的支撑。
