turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I've mentioned Figma a couple times here so I don't want to beleaguer the point, but they're certainly a team that I've looked up to through my entire experience at Notion. We were kind of sibling companies in a way. Huge kudos to Claire Butler over there who I knew led all of those efforts and we would trade a lot of knowledge back and forth, which was so lovely to have that relationship. But they did an amazing job I think in a similar vein to Notion of saying, okay, people are really excited to create these things and then put them out there on the internet. So how can we just fuel that particular motion out there? The other example I'll give, which is a little bit of a different tack is Stripe. And when Stripe launched Stripe Atlas, not necessarily core to the initial product line that Stripe was known for and what had been foundational for them, but allowed them to build this community among probably their core demographic at the time, which was founders and startups that were growing through the stages to mid-market, they were able to cultivate this huge audience of founders around giving advice and providing them with resources to actually get started and do that zero to one journey. (00:32:22): So while it was adjacent to maybe what the company's core mission was, it allowed them to actually create community among their customer base because they were like, "We're knowledgeable. We can share these things with you that we know are core to your journey." So I would encourage anyone who's thinking about community that way to be like, "Oh, maybe it doesn't have to be around our product. So specifically. What other knowledge or resourcing can we offer to the people who we do want using our product that's going to be really instrumental for them and can we convene them around that idea?"
turns.zh: 我前面已经提过 Figma 好几次了，所以不想老调重弹，但它们确实是我在 Notion 整个经历里一直很佩服的团队。我们某种程度上算是兄弟公司。特别要向那边的 Claire Butler 致敬，我知道是她在主导所有那些动作，我们之间经常来回交流知识，能有那种关系真的很好。但它们做得很出色的一点，和 Notion 类似：就是“好，人们真的很兴奋能创造出这些东西，然后把它发到网上去。那我们怎么去给这种态势加把火？”我要给的另一个例子，角度稍微不同，是 Stripe。当 Stripe 推出 Stripe Atlas 时——那不一定是其核心产品线，Stripe 成名靠的、作为基石的都不是这个——但它让他们能在当时可能最核心的人群里建起社区，也就是那些从初创一路长到中端市场的创始人和创业公司。他们得以围绕“给建议、提供资源帮人真正起步、走完从 0 到 1”这件事，培养出一大批创始人受众。(00:32:22)所以虽然这跟公司的核心使命算是相邻，但它让他们真的在客户群里建起了社区，因为他们就像在说“我们懂行，我们可以把这些对你这段旅程至关重要的东西分享给你”。所以我会鼓励任何这样思考社区的人去想：“哦，也许它不一定非要围绕我们的产品本身。我们还能给那些我们确实想要用我们产品的人，提供什么别的知识或资源，对他们真的很有用？我们能不能围绕那个想法把他们聚起来？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm noticing a strong correlation between legendary generational companies, Figma, Stripe, Notion and community efforts and building community. That's interesting.
turns.zh: 我注意到，那些传奇的、一代代传下去的公司——Figma、Stripe、Notion——和社区动作、建社区之间，有很强的相关性。这挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes. I'm a big proponent. At the same time I don't think that community is right for every company. I think that there is definitely an analysis to run on that. But hopefully this is helpful for those who can identify that those are attributes they have.
turns.zh: 对。我是大力拥护者。但与此同时，我不觉得社区适合每一家公司。我觉得这绝对是要做一番分析的。不过希望这对那些能认出自己具备这些特质的人有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To pull on a thread there, what are maybe thoughts for when it probably doesn't make sense to invest a lot of efforts into building a community around your product? We talked a little bit about high-end enterprise products. Is there anything else that just like, man, it's probably not worth your time?
turns.zh: 顺着这条线拉一下，那什么时候大概不适合在你的产品周围投入大量精力去建社区？我们聊了一点高端企业级产品。还有没有别的，会让人觉得“天，这大概不值得你花时间”？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Like I said, if it's more of a sales led culture that you have, which is definitely true of products that are a little bit pricier or that require longer contracts, so understanding that. But I do think the community takes on different forms and I think when you hear the word community, you think of a big forum of some type, whether it's a Slack instance or something else where people are chatting away all day long. And I don't think it has to be that. That's not the only representation of it. So if you think about what is going to be right for you at any given time, I actually created this two by two matrix, which maybe I'll share with you after this. And on the axis you have, whether you have hit product market fit or if you're still exploring product market set and then whether you're strongly enterprise or strongly consumer. And based on where you land in that two by two matrix, there's a form of community or a community related initiative that could be right for you. (00:34:31): So just to give you an example of maybe an extremely different form factor from Notion, let's say that you're still on your way to product market fit and you're a strongly enterprise oriented product. I think that you have the opportunity to do customer advisory boards, which is really convening even smaller circles of ideal fit users and making sure that they are connected to each other as well as you, and then incentivize to provide you with feedback. Understanding that they're really on the ground floor of this journey with you and that they're going to be able to have influence over whatever you do in the future. Those folks can end up growing into your biggest evangelists and I've seen that happen a number of times and I would still consider that community even though maybe that is not what comes to mind for folks.
turns.zh: 就像我说的，如果你更多的是销售驱动的文化——对那些贵一点、或者需要更长合同的产品肯定是这样——那要理解这一点。但我确实觉得社区会以不同的形式存在，而当你听到“社区”这个词，你会想到某个大论坛，不管是 Slack 实例还是别的什么，人们整天在那儿聊个不停。但我觉得它不一定非得那样，那不是它唯一的形态。所以如果你去想某个时刻什么对你是对的，我其实做了一张 2×2 的矩阵，也许聊完我分享给你。横轴纵轴是：你到底是已经达成了产品市场契合，还是还在探索产品市场契合；以及你是强企业级还是强消费者。根据你落在这张 2×2 矩阵的哪个格子，就有一种社区、或一个跟社区相关的动作可能是适合你的。(00:34:31)举个跟 Notion 形态差别极大的例子：假设你还在通往产品市场契合的路上，而且你是强企业级导向的产品。我觉得你有机会去做客户顾问委员会（customer advisory boards），也就是把更小的、理想契合的用户圈子聚起来，确保他们既彼此相连、也跟你相连，然后用激励让他们给你反馈。要理解，他们是跟你一起在这段旅程最底层的，他们能对你未来做的任何事产生影响。那些人最后会变成你最大的传播者，这种事我见过好几次了，而且我仍然会把那算作社区，尽管那可能不是人们脑子里第一时间想到的社区。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well I imagine that becomes the seed of a community that you eventually build. Let's definitely link to this in the show notes. Can you give maybe a couple more examples of this grid? So that was pre-product market fit and then what was the other?
turns.zh: 嗯，我猜那会变成你最终要建的那个社区的种子。我们一定要在节目笔记里放这个链接。你能再给几张这个矩阵的例子吗？刚才那个是“未达产品市场契合”，那另一个是什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Strongly enterprise.
turns.zh: 强企业级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Enterprise. Okay, cool. Yeah, what are a couple other of the elements of this grid?
turns.zh: 企业级。好，酷。那这个矩阵还有哪几个要素？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: So if you're strongly enterprise and you have product market fit, let's say, this is something that Notion has really benefited from, but really emphasizing the champions in the consultants communities. So the folks who, like I said, may be inside of your customers who really get it, really get your value, really are excited to help you land and expand perhaps inside of their companies, making sure that they have a place to gather and a place to feel like they are more connected with your team than the average person gets to be. That they are special and that they have access. And then on the consultant side, like I said, just making it really easy, removing friction, helping promote the folks who want to be out there, helping you succeed with more customers. Like Salesforce. I know that this is a golden oldie of an example, but if you talk to anybody who was really early at Salesforce, they really went into this where they saw people emerging who wanted to help other companies. This layer of people who didn't work at Salesforce but saw the opportunity to help other companies actually succeed with it, implement it, grow with it, and that's become a massive part of Salesforce's model. And so if you're in that quadrant, figuring out how to start moving people in your customer base into those categories.
turns.zh: 所以如果你是强企业级、而且你达成了产品市场契合，假设——这正是 Notion 很受益的一点——那就真的要强调 champions 和顾问社区。也就是我说的，那些可能在你客户内部、真的懂行、真的懂你的价值、真的兴奋于能帮你在他们公司里落地和扩张的人，要确保他们有个聚集的地方，让他们觉得自己比普通人更能跟你的团队连在一起。让他们觉得自己特别、有特权。然后在顾问那一侧，就像我说的，就是让一切都真的容易、消除摩擦、帮那些想走出去的人做推广，帮你在更多客户身上成功。像 Salesforce。我知道这是个老掉牙的例子，但如果你去跟任何很早期在 Salesforce 的人聊，他们真的就是这么干的——他们看到有人冒出来想帮别的公司。这一层人并不在 Salesforce 工作，但他们看到了帮别的公司真正用它成功、实施它、跟它一起成长的机会，而这已经成了 Salesforce 模式里极大的一块。所以如果你在那个象限，就要想清楚怎么开始把你客户群里的这些人往那些类别里推。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is awesome. Maybe let's do one more of this grid and then we'll leave one for people to click into and check it out.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。这张矩阵咱们也许再来一个，然后留一个让人点进去自己看。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I'll talk about Notion's quadrant, which is the one that I would put up and to the right, which is you have product market fit and you're maybe a little bit closer to the consumer side of the spectrum. Obviously Notion runs the full gamut, but I would say especially early on I think that that's where we saw things take root and that's where I think ambassadors and influencers really take off. Individuals who are going to be extremely vocal, extremely excited, and where you're going to see more of this wildfire spread, at least trying the product, using the product, understanding what the product is. So if you can try to fuel that type of motion if you're in that quadrant, that's helpful.
turns.zh: 我来说说 Notion 的象限，就是我会放在右上方那个：你已经达成了产品市场契合，而且可能稍微偏消费者这一侧。当然 Notion 是全覆盖的，但我会说尤其在早期，我觉得就是那个格子让我们看到事情扎下了根，也是那个格子让大使和红人真正起飞。那些人会特别爱发声、特别兴奋，而你会在那里看到更多这种野火般的蔓延——至少会去试用产品、用产品、搞懂产品是什么。所以如果你在那个象限，能去给这种态势加把火，是有帮助的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to this ambassador program real quick because it feels like something that a lot of people talk about and can do and especially in this quadrant of product market fit and consumer. How does this work? Is it you select, here's 100 ambassadors we're going to pick because we think they're awesome and they're great examples of people using, say, Notion and then we're just going to provide them with all the help they need to be successful with Notion. How do you think about creating an ambassador program?
turns.zh: 我想很快回到大使计划，因为它感觉是很多人都在聊、也都能做的事，尤其在“已达成产品市场契合 + 消费者”这个象限。这到底怎么运作？是你去挑选，比如“这是我们要选的 100 个大使，因为我们觉得他们超棒、是用 Notion 的绝佳范例”，然后我们就给他们所有需要的帮助、让他们在 Notion 上成功？你是怎么思考打造一个大使计划的？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I actually think it's pretty analogous to when you're thinking about positioning your company because I think the best first step for any positioning exercise is to think who are our best fit customers? And it's not necessarily who we wish they would be, but it's actually the hard cold reality of who they actually are. Where it's like these are the people that seem to be really getting it. They're paying us more, they're talking about it just organically. So really figuring out everything about who they are and making sure that those are the people that you're actually inviting in early. So the initial base of the ambassadors program which started back in 2019 was just 20 people and they were the 20 people who we happened to see be the most vocal already across Twitter and a couple of other social media platforms because they had that shared quality of wanting to be really vocal and expressive about their experience with the product. So that would be my advice for how to get one of these rolling.
turns.zh: 我其实觉得它跟你给公司做定位（positioning）很像，因为我觉得任何定位工作最好的第一步，就是想：谁是我们最契合的客户？而不一定是我们希望他们成为的样子，而是他们实际上到底是谁的那个冷酷现实。就像：这些就是看起来真的搞懂了的人。他们付我们更多钱，他们在自发地聊它。所以真的把关于他们的一切搞清楚，并确保那些就是你最早邀请进来的人。所以大使计划最初在 2019 年启动时，只有 20 个人，他们就是我们在 Twitter 和另外几个社交平台上碰巧看到已经最爱发声的那 20 个人，因为他们有那种共同特质：想对自己的产品体验特别大声、特别有表达欲地讲出来。所以那会是我对一个大使计划怎么启动的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then what do you do for them?
turns.zh: 那然后你为他们做些什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Definitely making sure that there's enough incentive built in, right? Because like we said, it's not meant to be a transactional relationship, but we want them to feel like they are having a special experience, that they are connected with the company in a unique way. And it was so interesting to us how giving them the preview of features was so motivating to them and being able to use them and then give us feedback and feel really heard by the product team. So that was a big area of focus and I know that that still is and it's become even more of a robust conversation between the community and the team at Notion itself. (00:39:52): And then also we would do these very special experiences where Ivan or Akshay or Simon or MLM who's the head of engineering there would be available for these conversations where they would answer questions and it would feel like a very proprietary space. I think that that was really interesting to people. And then of course the things that you would suspect around subsidizing events. Making sure that people felt that they were actually supported by us to throw these events. And then also promoting their work. So if you look back at the social media channels, so much of the focus is on putting the creations of the people we were working with front and center as opposed to talking about just what the company was up to.
turns.zh: 肯定要确保里面有足够多的激励，对吧？因为就像我们说的，它本意不是交易关系，但我们想让他们觉得自己有了一段特别的体验，以一种独特的方式跟公司连在一起。而让我们特别感兴趣的是，给他们抢先体验功能，对他们居然那么有驱动力——他们能用上、然后给我们反馈、觉得自己真的被产品团队听到了。所以那是一个很大的焦点，我知道现在依然是，而且它已经变成了 Notion 社区和团队之间更扎实的对话。(00:39:52)另外我们还会搞那些特别体验，比如 Ivan、Akshay、Simon，或者工程负责人 MLM，会腾出时间来参加这些对话、回答问题，让人感觉那是个很专属的空间。我觉得那对人们来说真的很有意思。当然还有你预想得到的那些——补贴活动。确保人们觉得我们真的在支持他们办这些活动。还有推广他们的作品。所以如果你回看那些社交媒体频道，很多焦点都是把我们合作对象的创作放在最前面、中心位置，而不是只聊公司在忙什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you ever written about just how to design an ambassador program or has anyone written about how Notion did this? Because this is really interesting.
turns.zh: 你有没有写过怎么设计大使计划，或者有没有人写过 Notion 是怎么做的？因为这真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I don't know if anything has been written or went into all of this detail, but it was truly one of the more magical and I think still is one of the more magical parts of this entire endeavor. And now that team is three people. So Ben who's still there doing amazing things, Francisco who joined us in 2021. Or sorry at the end of 2020. And then Emma. And they are just all day every day talking to people around the whole world. The international component of this is also just completely wild to see.
turns.zh: 我不知道有没有人写过、或者写到过这么细，但这真的是整个事情里最神奇的部分之一，而且我觉得现在依然是最神奇的部分之一。现在那个团队是三个人。就是 Ben，还在那儿做着很棒的事；Francisco，2021 年加入的——不对，是 2020 年底；还有 Emma。他们就是整天整天地跟全世界的人聊。国际这一块也让人看得特别震撼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This could be a future First Round Review post, which we'll talk a bit about.
turns.zh: 这说不定能成为未来 First Round Review 的一篇稿子，我们待会儿会聊到一点。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes. Perhaps.
turns.zh: 对。也许吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question about this segment. Say someone is convinced they want to start investing in community and we talked about this two by two, but maybe just broadly if you had to boil it down to two or three pieces of advice for founders, for teams thinking about investing in community led growth and community in general, what would be some of those pieces of advice?
turns.zh: 这段最后一个问题。假设有人已经被说服、想开始投社区，我们也聊了那张 2×2。但更宽泛地说，如果你必须把它浓缩成给创始人、给想投社区驱动增长和社区本身的团队的两三条建议，那会是什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I don't know if you want to link to this in the show notes as well, but I actually put together some commandments for community builders.
turns.zh: 我不知道你想不想也在节目笔记里放这个链接，但我其实给社区建设者整理了一些“戒律”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ooh. Absolutely.
turns.zh: 噢，当然要放。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Some alliteration. So the thing that I think were very defining for us early on, I already mentioned something about this, but not trying to hit a number early on. So don't dilute the impact of what it is that you're trying to do in order to show growth. I think that that's very important to protect yourself early on. So making sure that you are learning what individuals really want out of this and making them feel like they're very seen and very heard. That was a big area of focus and I think it's what kept people really engaged and coming back and feeling like this was a secondary family for them. And then one of the things that was most interesting to us that once we started sharing what was going on in the community with folks at Notion. So we would do this during all Hands meetings or on Slack, Ben would post these really incredible updates of just all of the activities of people in the community and what they were up to every month. (00:42:46): And it was just so inspiring for everybody inside the company that I think it all rallied us to do even more, I guess, day to day and really understand who it was we were building for.
turns.zh: 来点押韵吧。所以有几条对我们早期特别有定义作用的——这点我已经提过一点——就是早期别去冲一个数字。也就是说，不要为了显示增长，而稀释了你真正想做的事的影响力。我觉得在早期保护好这一点非常重要。所以要确保你在了解每个人真正想从这个社区得到什么，让他们觉得自己真的被看见、被听到。那是一个很大的焦点，我觉得那正是让人们真的投入、一直回来、觉得这里像第二个家的原因。然后最让我们感兴趣的一件事之一是：一旦我们开始在公司内部跟 Notion 的人分享社区里在发生什么。我们会在全员会上、或者在 Slack 上做这件事，Ben 会发那些特别棒的月度更新，就是社区里大家在干嘛、忙些什么。(00:42:46)那对公司里每个人来说都特别鼓舞人心，我觉得它让我们所有人都更齐心，在日常里想做更多，也更真的理解了我们到底是在为谁打造。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any other commandments you would add for if you already have a community going? If you have something bubbling for things you should do to keep it healthy and consistently good and growing?
turns.zh: 对那些已经在运营社区的人，你还会再补充什么戒律吗？如果你已经有东西在冒泡了，为了保持它健康、稳定地好、并且增长，你该做些什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. I mean this is going to be a little contrarian perhaps, and I mean this is just one data point for me, but not growing it so big so fast. One thing that we actually thought about pretty carefully was what a rate of healthy growth would be. So there actually is an application process for joining the ambassadors. It's a very light application process and it really is just so that we know how many people are interested in this. And then they're inducted around ... I think at the time it was 20 people at a time every month. So that it wouldn't feel like all of a sudden this had changed in terms of how the interactions were feeling, but rather gave everybody time to welcome the new people in and get to know them. And one of Ben and I's favorite things ever about working at Notion I think was when we would induct new people into the ambassadors and they would introduce themselves and say, "Hey, I am from Venezuela and here's the ways in which notion has changed my life."
turns.zh: 对。我是说这也许有点反共识，而且对我个人来说这也只是个例，但不要让它长得太快太大。我们其实很认真地想过，什么是健康的增长率。所以加入大使其实有个申请流程。那是个很轻量的申请流程，真的只是为了让我们知道有多少人对这感兴趣。然后他们大概以……我记得当时是每个月 20 个人一批这样被接纳进来。这样就不会让人突然觉得互动的氛围变了，而是给了每个人时间去欢迎新人、去认识他们。我觉得 Ben 和我，在 Notion 工作最爱的时刻之一，就是我们接纳新人进大使计划、他们做自我介绍的时候，比如有人说“嘿，我来自委内瑞拉，Notion 是这样改变了我的生活”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: "I'm from Hong Kong and here's how it's changed my life." And all of that was just so fulfilling. That would be the number one thing I would say is give your community time to actually grow in what feels like an organic fashion as well. Because I think ironically, and then I'll stop rambling about this, but if you grow to something like, oh we have 5,000 ambassadors, which feels really good to say on a website, the conversation is actually very muted. I think because people feel like they're speaking to an auditorium whenever they say anything. I think it's because you don't really have a sense of who else is there with you. So helping to defray those concerns I think is a good course of action.
turns.zh: “我来自香港，它是这样改变了我的生活。”那些都让人特别有满足感。所以我要说的头号建议，就是也给你的社区时间去真正以一种有机的方式生长。因为我觉得，反过来说——我就啰嗦到这儿——如果你长到比如“噢我们有 5000 个大使”，在网站上说出来感觉特好，但对话其实变得非常冷清。我觉得那是因为人们每次开口，都觉得自己是在对着一个礼堂讲话。我想是因为你根本感觉不到还有谁跟你在一起。所以帮着化解这些顾虑，我觉得是妥当的做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've seen the same thing with the growth rate being really important with my newsletter Slack community. I think most listeners probably know this, but if you're a paid newsletter subscriber, you get access to the Slack community. There's about 10,000 people in there. And I find the filter of people that are willing to pay for content like a newsletter is a really good filter for awesome people. And so it ends up slowing growth in a really healthy way and then just creating this filter of the people that really want to self-improve and value the sort of thing join, and it becomes a really amazing group of people.
turns.zh: 我在我 newsletter 的 Slack 社区上也看到过同样的事——增长率真的很重要。我想大多数听众可能都知道，但如果你是付费 newsletter 订户，就能进那个 Slack 社区。里面大概有 1 万人。而我发现，愿意为像 newsletter 这样的内容付费的人，这个过滤器特别好，能筛出很棒的人。于是它以一种非常健康的方式放慢了增长，然后就自然形成了一个过滤器，只留下那些真的想自我提升、看重这类东西、会主动加入的人，最后就成了一个特别棒的群体。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. It feels like such a ... I don't know. There's an emotional quality to it I think when that's the case. And all of those people end up being so incredibly impactful. The last point I'll make about community at Notion is that a lot of those people, and we actually ended up launching I think a channel for folks who wanted to do this in particular, but run communities external to Notion's actual owned communities. So you end up with Facebook groups that have ... I think Notion in Vietnam has like 250,000 members. Or the subreddit, which I now know has 210,000 people in the Notion subreddit. And those are all run and moderated by community members who just love running their own communities.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得那种情况下，有一种……我说不清。但有一种情感上的质地。而那些人最后都产生了难以置信的影响力。关于 Notion 社区我要说的最后一点是：那些人里很多——我们其实后来还专门开了一个频道给那些特别想这么做的人——他们在 Notion 自己拥有的社区之外，运营着外部的社区。于是你就有了 Facebook 群组——我想 Notion 在越南的群组大概有 25 万成员。还有那个 subreddit，我现在知道 Notion 的 subreddit 里有 21 万人。而那些全都是由就是爱运营自己社区的成员在跑、在维护。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you've achieved your OKRs of ubiquity of Notion.
turns.zh: 我觉得你达成了 Notion “无处不在”的 OKR 了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes. It was always a value at Notion to make sure that we were reaching as many people as possible.
turns.zh: 对。确保我们触达尽可能多的人，这一直是 Notion 的一个价值观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's working. One tactical question. Where does the own community of Notion live? Is it a Slack? Is it an online thing you've built yourself?
turns.zh: 起作用了。一个战术问题。Notion 自己的社区在哪？是个 Slack 吗？还是你们自己搭的线上东西？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: It is in Slack. And the thinking there, and it still is, was that we really just wanted to be in the course of people's everyday lives. We didn't want to be this other destination that you would have to make a point to going to every day.
turns.zh: 是在 Slack 里。当时的想法——现在也还是——就是我们真的只想待在人们日常生活的动线里。我们不想成为那种你每天还得特意跑过去的目的地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly how I thought about it with my newsletter Slack community. PMs and founders, they're already in Slack all day. And just that badge, being on the app telling them there's something to check is such a powerful feature versus download a whole new app or go to a whole new website, you're never going to go there. It has to be 10 times better to pull you to a whole new site and change your habits.
turns.zh: 我对我的 newsletter Slack 社区也是这么想的。产品经理和创始人，他们整天都在 Slack 里。而仅仅是那个徽标、那个在 app 上告诉他们“有东西要查看”的提示，就是个特别强大的功能——相比让你下载一个全新的 app、或者去一个全新的网站，你根本不会去。要把你拉到一个全新站点、改变你的习惯，它得比现在好上 10 倍才行。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I absolutely agree.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad we're all on Slack. Slack's so underrated. I feel like people hate on Slack all the time, but it's such a good product.
turns.zh: 很高兴我们都在 Slack 上。Slack 被严重低估了。我感觉大家总在吐槽 Slack，但它真的是个好产品。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: We all love it. It's just becomes something we take for granted in the background there.
turns.zh: 我们都爱它。它只是变成了我们在后台当理所当然的那样东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Okay. This is a good time to shift to our second topic, which is around content and content marketing. So you started the First Round Review at First Round?
turns.zh: 对，没错。好。这是个转向下一个话题的好时机，也就是内容、内容营销。所以你是在 First Round 创办了 First Round Review 吗？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you know this, but First Round Review was a big part of my early trajectory with this newsletter life. I did a guest post in the First Round Review and that was-
turns.zh: 我不知道你知不知道，但 First Round Review 是我走上 newsletter 这条路早期轨迹里很重要的一块。我在 First Round Review 上发过一篇客座文章，那次是——

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I remember this.
turns.zh: 我记得这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was a huge deal for me. That was my first 500 subscribers to my newsletter.
turns.zh: 那对我来说是件大事。那是我 newsletter 的前 500 个订户。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then I did another guest post down the road, but that was not as important. It was a big part of my early path down this life. And so thank you for creating that platform. I was very honored to be involved.
turns.zh: 后来我又发过一篇客座文章，但那篇没那么重要。它是我走上这条路的早期很重要的一部分。所以谢谢你创造了那个平台。能参与进去，我深感荣幸。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: That's fantastic to hear and exactly what we wanted to have happen. Just extraordinary operators being given a platform and then using it to do whatever it is that they wanted to do. That was part of the dream always.
turns.zh: 听到这个太棒了，这也正是我们想要的。就是让那些出色的操盘手有一个平台，然后拿它去做他们自己想做的事。那一直都是这个梦想的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's working.
turns.zh: 起作用了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. I'm thrilled because now people are learning so much from you.
turns.zh: 对。我特别开心，因为现在人们能从你身上学到这么多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's an inspiration for where when I started too, just I wish I could be as good as the First Round Review and the stuff just keeps coming and coming. It's amazing. And I know other folks run it now. I don't know if they want to be named. They like to be behind the scenes.
turns.zh: 对。它对我起步时也是个鼓舞，我只是希望自己能像 First Round Review 那么好，而且好内容源源不断。太厉害了。我知道现在换别人在运营了。我不知道他们想不想被点名。他们喜欢待在幕后。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: They do, but I'm going to shout them out anyway because they do such an extraordinary job. I mean, Jessi Craige Shikman over there has been doing this now for longer than I did and she is absolutely incredible and her team is extraordinary and I don't miss it every single time it comes out.
turns.zh: 他们确实在运营，但不管怎样我都要喊他们出来，因为他们做得太出色了。我是说，那边的 Jessi Craige Shikman 做这个的时间比我还长，她绝对厉害，她的团队也非凡，每期出来我都不会错过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I tried to thank her my post. She's like, "Don't mention that. I'm behind the scenes."
turns.zh: 对。我在我的帖子想谢谢她。她说“别提这个。我就在幕后”。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Maybe I'll ask her.
turns.zh: 也许我去问她一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We have to give her some cred somehow.
turns.zh: 我们总得用某种方式给她点 credit。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. She deserves it.
turns.zh: 对，当然。她值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So kind of zooming out, content marketing, maybe just to give some examples of just what are some of the most impactful things you've been a part of that come from creating content? Whether it's Notion, First Round, anywhere else, what are some examples?
turns.zh: 所以稍微拉远一点看，内容营销——能不能举些例子，你参与过的、由创作内容带来的最有影响力的东西？不管是 Notion、First Round，还是别处，有哪些例子？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah, I'll give a few examples. Obviously First Round is a huge example and so I'd be remiss in not going into some detail there. And truly that was a team effort from the very beginning. I joined in 2013 and again, I was just so fortunate to work with a leader who believed in it from the very beginning. Josh Kopelman, who's the partner there who was just a massive supporter of mine. Phin Barnes on the partnership team. But then particularly Brett Burson who was running the platform team, which is where all of these value added services lived. (00:49:40): So it was me and an events person and the talent person and Brett just gave us all of the runway and all of the belief and support that we needed. And he was really bullish on content and really helped from the beginning, connecting me with incredible interview subjects. Because this whole thing, the only reason I think it survived and did as well as it did is that we were able to land a few really big names at the very beginning. And then of course that helps you down the road whenever you're trying to convince anyone else to do it because you say so and so and so and so have already been featured. So that was I think just a big point of confidence and also tactically, for anyone out there thinking about it, if they can leverage whatever connections they have in that vein.
turns.zh: 好，我给几个例子。First Round 显然是个大例子，所以我不细说就失职了。真的从一开始这就是个团队努力。我 2013 年加入，再说一次，我很幸运能跟一个从一开始就相信这事的领导共事。Josh Kopelman，那边的一位合伙人，是我的超级支持者。还有合作团队的 Phin Barnes。但尤其要提 Brett Burson，他当时管平台团队，所有那些增值服务都在那个团队里。(00:49:40)所以是我在、一个做活动的、一个管人才的，Brett 给了我们所有人需要的空间、信任和支持。他对内容特别看好，从一开始就帮了大忙，帮我把我连到那些特棒的采访对象上。因为整件事——我觉得它能活下来、而且做得那么好，唯一的理由就是我们在最开始能请到几个真正的大咖。然后当然这帮你往后走，每当你想说服别人来做时就有底气，因为你可以说“某某某、某某某都已经上过了”。所以我觉得那既是很大的信心来源，也是一个战术点：对任何在考虑这事的人，如果他们能借上那方面的人脉就用上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was at dinner with Brett yesterday.
turns.zh: 我昨天跟 Brett 一起吃晚饭了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Oh my god. What a guy, right?
turns.zh: 我的天。那家伙真行，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First Round event. What a guy. That guy's amazing. I'm a huge fan. He's built an incredible platform and program at First Round.
turns.zh: First Round 的活动。真行。那家伙太神了。我超级粉他。他在 First Round 搭出了一个不可思议的平台和项目。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: And he's one of the people that I've learned the most from, certainly. But more specific to your question around what the content program was able to do there, certainly discovery of First Round. I think prior to that it was a very successful VC fund, but I think we got in front of all kinds of people, particularly in non-traditional geographies or non-traditional founder types or all of that. People who are inside large companies like Google, Apple, Amazon, whenever we would look at our list of subscribers, we had an disproportionate number of email addresses within those companies that were clearly curious about the startup experience. And I think First Round Review was helpful in moving them more toward that mindset and then them obviously understanding that First Round would be a great first stop for them.
turns.zh: 而他肯定也是我从中学习最多的人之一。但更具体地回到你那个问题——那个内容项目在那儿能做成什么——毫无疑问是 First Round 的“被发现”。我觉得在那之前它就是个很成功的 VC 基金，但我觉得我们走到了各种各样的人面前，尤其是那些非传统地域、或非传统创始人类型的人。那些在大公司里的人，像 Google、Apple、Amazon，每当我们看我们的订户名单，这些公司里的邮箱地址占比高得不成比例，显然他们对创业经历很好奇。而我觉得 First Round Review 帮着把他们往那种心态上推，然后他们显然就明白，First Round 会是他们很好的第一站。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What would you say is key to content being valuable? So you're talking about the First Round Review became really effective for people learning about First Round, working with First Round, discovery of First Round, but it's not just with content you just write some stuff and it works. It doesn't work that way. What have you learned about just what do you have to get right? You mentioned have names people recognize. Is there anything else you've learned over the years of just like, here's what we need to get right if you're trying to use content as a way to create discovery and awareness of your stuff?
turns.zh: 你会说内容有价值的关键是什么？你在说 First Round Review 对让人们了解 First Round、跟 First Round 合作、发现 First Round 变得很有效，但内容不是你随便写点东西就管用。不是那样运作的。你学到了什么——到底得把什么做对？你提到了要有人们认得的大咖。这么多年下来，如果你要用内容来给你的东西创造“被发现”和认知度，还有什么别的你学到的——也就是我们得把什么做对？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: This is something that I think we chatted about briefly, but the way that you think about product market fit, you have to think about content market fit. So even though content feels like it's running adjacent to the actual product that you're putting out there, you still have to think about who is my audience? Who is the audience that I really want to have? Who is the audience that is going to be drawn to this most? Who are they? What is it that they really need in their lives? Even abstracting content from it at all. What is it that they need to get promoted? What is it that they need to avoid failure? What is it that causes them a great deal of anxiety in the day-to-day of their lives or their work? And can you create some type of content product that is going to address this for them and is actually going to have that value? (00:52:36): So I think approaching content the way that you would a product in a lot of ways is very instructive way to sort of start hashing out your strategy. Starting with your audience, understanding their big needs. You've heard this, I'm sure, and most of your audience has, but there's the vitamin versus painkiller dichotomy. And painkillers always win. So can your content be a painkiller? Can it help people out of situations that are causing them a lot of pain? Can it help people stop being so confused or can it make them even feel less alone in their experience? That was a big one for First Round Review is helping operators share failures or suboptimal situations in the spirit of helping many other people feel like that was normalized and that the experiences they were having weren't as dire as maybe they had thought.
turns.zh: 这是咱们简单聊过一点的，但说到产品市场契合（product market fit），你还得想想内容市场契合（content market fit）。所以尽管内容看起来像是跟你推出去的那款实际产品并行存在的东西，你仍然得想清楚：我的受众是谁？我真正想要的是哪一群受众？哪一群受众最容易被它吸引？他们到底是什么人？他们在生活里真正需要的是什么？哪怕把内容本身完全抽离出来。他们需要在职场上获得晋升，需要避免失败，需要在日常的工作和生活里少一点焦虑——这些又是什么？而你能否做出某种内容产品，去真正解决他们的这些需求、真的有那个价值？(00:52:36)所以我觉得，在很多时候用你对待一款产品的方式去对待内容，是理清你策略一个很有指导意义的起点。从你的受众开始，理解他们的大需求。你肯定听过，你的听众大多数也听过，就是“维生素 vs 止痛药”的那个二分法。而止痛药永远赢。所以你的内容能当一剂止痛药吗？它能帮人们脱离那些让他们很痛的处境吗？它能帮人们不再那么困惑，或者能让他们在经历里觉得自己不那么孤单吗？对 First Round Review 来说，很大的一点就是帮操盘手分享失败、或者不那么理想的处境，本着让更多其他人觉得“这很正常”、他们正在经历的没自己想的那么糟的精神。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. It connects so much with the way I think about writing. I use the jobs to be done framework a little bit here where I'm just like, what job am I doing when I'm writing a post? And you tell me if this makes sense to you, but I feel like there's four jobs to be done of a newsletter. Either how people make money. There's newsletters, here's how to invest, here's how to buy Bitcoin and win. How people make money. Entertain people. There's a lot of funny things, memes and cartoons and things like that. How people get better at their work or life, which is the category we're in. And then inform people. Like news.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。它跟我思考写作的方式太相通了。我在这儿有点用“待办工作”（jobs to be done）的框架，就是我会想：我写一篇帖子时，是在完成什么工作？你看看这对你通不通——我觉得一个 newsletter 有四种待办工作。一是人们怎么赚钱。有些 newsletter 就是“怎么投资”“怎么买比特币赢”。人们怎么赚钱。二是娱乐人们。有很多好玩的事、梗图、漫画之类的。三是人们怎么把工作生活变得更好，这也是我们所在的类别。四是告知人们。比如新闻。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes. What they didn't know before. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。就是他们之前不知道的。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it feels like you got to do really well. You got to pick which bucket you're in. And let me know if you can think of any others because these are the four that I always come back to. And then pick your bucket and then it's be the best at that thing in your category. The way I think about it.
turns.zh: 而且感觉你得做得真的好。你得选自己在哪个桶里。如果你还能想到别的，告诉我，因为这四个是我一直会回到的基本盘。然后选好你的桶，接下来就是在你那个类别里，成为这件事上最好的。我是这么想的。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I love that listing out of those and also the acknowledgement that there are emotional jobs to be done. That there are not just utilitarian jobs to be done. It's not just, you didn't know this before and now you do, but it's like you felt this way before and now you don't or you do. And I think that that's underestimated. So I love that you called out entertaining people because we're all working in an industry where it's wonderful to interact with some of that sparkle and levity. So I love that approach.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你把那些列出来，也喜欢你承认还有“情感上的待办工作”。不只是功利的待办工作。不只是“你之前不知道、现在知道了”，而是“你之前是那种感受、现在不是了、或者现在是了”。我觉得这点被低估了。所以我喜欢你点出“娱乐人们”，因为我们都在一个行业里，能跟那种闪光和轻松互动，是很美妙的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And something else that goes unsaid I think in the way you talked about this is just putting in the time to make it really high quality. If you look at a First Round post, how much time would you say goes into in the typical First Round Review post?
turns.zh: 还有一点，我觉得你聊这个的时候没明说，就是投入时间去把它做得真的很高质。你看一篇 First Round 的帖子，一篇典型的 First Round Review 文章，你觉得大概要投入多少时间？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Oh gosh. Here's where I'm going to shout out my writing partner at First Round, Sean Young, who was there with me for most of my time there and he and I would always, always talk about this. But it would take eight hours to just write the thing. And that's after you had done all of the prep work of making sure that your interviewee was feeling really anchored and understanding a topic that you were both really excited about and making sure you were mining all of the tactical gems from that conversation. And then you would start writing and that would be another eight hours. I don't know if that's your experience, but certainly was ours.
turns.zh: 噢天。这里我要喊出我在 First Round 的写作搭档 Sean Young，他跟我在一起待了大半段时间，他和我总是、总是在聊这个。光写那篇东西就得花八个小时。而且那还是在你做完所有准备工作之后——确保受访者觉得很有底气、对你们俩都真的兴奋的某个话题很理解，还要确保你从那场对话里挖出了所有战术性的宝石。然后你才开始写，那又是八个小时。我不知道你是不是这种体验，但对我们来说确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, very similar. I don't tie myself, but I feel like the median time to write a post for me is about 10 hours.
turns.zh: 对，非常像。我没给自己计时，但我感觉我写一篇帖子的中位时间大概是 10 个小时。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's I think the key that a lot of people don't think about. One is they don't have the time, and two, they don't realize they should spend this much time because the bar's so high for content on the internet as we all know. There's so much stuff out there. And so to get above that noise you have to really make it really good and that just takes time. And I find this really strong correlation between the time it takes me to write a post and how well it does. It's very highly correlated. And the advantage folks like say the First Round Review have and I have is I do this and there's a team doing this. And so people that are doing this on the side, it's much harder because they don't have that time.
turns.zh: 而这我觉得是很多人没想到的关键。一是他们没那个时间，二是他们没意识到自己该花这么多时间，因为就像我们都知道，网上内容的门槛太高了。外面有太多东西了。所以要盖过那个噪音，你得真的把它做得很好，而那就要花时间。我发现我写一篇帖子花的时间和它表现得多好之间，有很强的相关性。相关性非常高。而像 First Round Review、还有我这样的人有的优势是，我在做、而且有一个团队在做。所以那些在业余做的人，难得多，因为他们没那个时间。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: It is. I end up admiring those people a lot where I'm like, how are you doing this?
turns.zh: 是啊。我最后会特别佩服那些人，会想：你们到底是怎么做到的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. They're sacrificing something.
turns.zh: 对。他们在牺牲别的东西。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. But truly, it's a very shared experience with you. And I think that a lot of that was making connections between the information that you had available from these interviews. So not just straight here's what this person said, but how can you draw connections between those things, connect the dots, pull out bigger themes. All of that is really where I think a lot of the time went.
turns.zh: 对。但说真的，这跟你是非常共通的体验。而我觉得那里面很多，是把你从这些访谈里得到的信息串起来。所以不只是“这个人说了什么”直白地放出来，而是你怎么在这些东西之间建立关联、连点成线、提炼出更大的主题。所有这些，我觉得才是大量时间真正花掉的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you said you had this content market fit questionnaire that you talked through. You're going to send me a link that we can point people to check it out, right?
turns.zh: 所以你说过你有一个聊过的“内容市场契合”问卷。你会发我一个链接，我们好指给人们去看，对吧？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome.
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Absolutely. A lot of it is about getting to know your audience to an almost beleaguered degree.
turns.zh: 当然。它很大一部分，是把了解你的受众做到一种几乎让人烦的程度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which is basically what job will you do for them, like you said. And so that makes sense. Maybe a couple more questions. Something that I've noticed a lot, and this is related to content and just PR and stuff like that. I've noticed a lot of people on Twitter and founders are trying to pitch this idea that you don't need to think about comms and press and PR as much because now you can go direct. You can have a newsletter, you can write, you can tweet, you can LinkedIn. Do you feel like that is where the future is going for founder press and comms and things like that or do you think you still need to have a really strong comms, press, PR org within your company?
turns.zh: 也就是基本上，就像你说的，你为他们完成的是什么工作。所以这说得通。也许再来几个问题。有一点我注意到很多，而且这跟内容、还有 PR 之类的东西有关。我注意到 Twitter 上很多、还有创始人，在试图兜售一个想法：你不需要那么考虑传播、媒体和 PR 了，因为现在你可以直接触达。你可以有 newsletter、可以写、可以发推、可以 LinkedIn。你觉得对创始人的媒体和传播这类事，未来的方向就是这样吗？还是你觉得你公司里仍然需要一个很强的传播、媒体、PR 组织？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: That's a great question because I think that there's been just a lot of change in this space over the last five years and certainly very strong opinions from all over the ecosystem. I'm a big believer in comms. And I don't just say that because I used to be a journalist or I used to work in comms. But I think that there are very few and far between incredible megaphones for what it is that you or your company is doing where you get to reach such a breadth of people with that stamp of credibility and notice. How do you get somebody to say, "Hey, this is really something you should pay attention to."? Obviously I support all of the owned media efforts that are really working and bubbling up. And like I said, influencer I think is going to be a massive shift in how we discover things, but maintaining a wonderful relationship with the press, being straightforward, being that brand that is going to be accessible, I really think that that pays off. (00:58:37): And just to give you one example, David Pierce, who I think is one of the best working journalists in tech today, he's at The Verge now. He was covering personal tech for the Wall Street Journal early on at Notion and published a story that said this is the one work-life productivity app that you'll ever need. And that was Notion's big break. Truly, if you look back at the graphs, that made a demonstrable difference. And I've seen that happen time and time again. And one of my other efforts at First Round was helping companies in the portfolio figure out how to DIY comm strategies. And I saw this again and again that the companies that did get stories that really told their mission, it made a big difference for just discovery awareness. The number of people who wanted to be involved with them as candidates, as investors, as customers.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题，因为我觉得这领域过去五年变化太大了，而且整个生态里各种强烈意见都有。我是传播（comms）的坚定信徒。我不只是因为自己以前是记者、或在传播部门干过才这么说。但我觉得，能让你或你的公司做的事被那样一个可信度盖章、被注意到、触达那么广人群的好喇叭，是极少极少的。你怎么让别人说“嘿，这真的是你该关注的东西”？显然我支持所有那些真正管用、在冒泡的自有媒体动作。而且就像我说的，我觉得红人会成为我们“发现东西”方式上一个巨大的转变，但跟媒体保持好关系、直来直去、做一个别人够得着的品牌，我真的觉得那是有回报的。(00:58:37)就给你一个例子：David Pierce，我觉得他是当今科技圈最优秀的在职记者之一，他现在在 The Verge。早期在 Notion 时，他在《华尔街日报》写个人科技，发了一篇稿子，说这是你这辈子唯一需要的那款工作生活效率 app。而那正是 Notion 的突破口。真的，你回头看那些曲线，那造成了明显的差别。而且这种事我一而再再而三地看到。我在 First Round 的另一项工作，是帮组合里的公司想清楚怎么 DIY 传播策略。我一而再再三地看到，那些真的讲出了自己使命、拿到了报道的公司，对“被发现”和认知度都造成了很大的差别。想以候选人、以投资人、以客户身份参与他们的人，数量都变了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This gives me a new post idea of just what are the big breaks of companies? What was the moment where they started taking off? Note to self?
turns.zh: 这倒给了我一个写新帖子的灵感——公司的那些突破口都是什么？它们开始起飞的那个瞬间是什么？记给自己？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes. The other big thing for the Notion was product hunts. I want to give them-
turns.zh: 对。Notion 另一件大事是 Product Hunt。我想给它们——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, okay. So posting on Product Hunt, that was a big deal for Notion.
turns.zh: 噢，好。所以在 Product Hunt 上发帖，对 Notion 来说是件大事。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: It was. And it remains a big deal. If you go on Product Hunt and you type in Notion, you'll see just how many templates have been able to get noted because of Product Hunt.
turns.zh: 是。而且至今仍是大事。如果你上 Product Hunt 打 Notion，你会看到有多少模板因为 Product Hunt 而被注意到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's the templates being posted, but then also the launch of Notion on Product Hunt?
turns.zh: 所以是模板被发上去，但还有 Notion 在 Product Hunt 上的发布？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yes. And Notion 2.0. And then whenever we would have a major productized launch.
turns.zh: 对。还有 Notion 2.0。然后每当我们有一个重大的产品化发布。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's awesome. Man, Product Hunt just keeps kicking.
turns.zh: 哇，太棒了。天，Product Hunt 真是长盛不衰。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Notion AI very recently for them, which couldn't be more exciting.
turns.zh: 对他们来说，最近的 Notion AI，没有比这更让人兴奋的了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have access to that. I've been playing around. It's awesome. Maybe a last question along these lines is thinking about the founders that you've worked with. So on the one hand you have Elon who is very direct on Twitter to his audience, and then Ivan feels much less so and more under the radar and doesn't love tweeting a lot. And then First Round Review somewhere in the middle. Do you have any thoughts on how much a founder should invest in, say, tweeting and going and communicating direct to folk? Or is it more just whatever the founder is, their personality, just go with that?
turns.zh: 我有那个的权限。我一直在玩。很厉害。也许顺着这条线最后一个问题，想想你合作过的那些创始人。一方面你有埃隆，他在 Twitter 上对他的受众非常直接；而 Ivan 感觉没那么直接，更低调，不太爱发推。然后 First Round Review 在中间某处。对于创始人应该投入多少在比如发推、直接跟大伙沟通上，你有什么看法？还是说更多就是“创始人是什么样的人、什么性格，就随他去”？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I really do think it's about personality and what feels authentic. I think that so much of a founder's strength comes from leaning into where they know that they love to work, what they know about themselves. And I think that one of the biggest mistakes you can make on social media is giving yourself a quota that you have to hit and say, I have to say X number of scintillating things every week on these platforms. We've just seen so much more traction, even from the main Notion accounts when we're a little bit more reserved and we wait until we have something to say that has value.
turns.zh: 我真的觉得这关乎性格、关乎什么感觉真实。我觉得创始人的力量很大一部分，来自倾身投入他们知道自己热爱工作、了解自己的地方。而我觉得在社交媒体上你能犯的最大错误之一，就是给自己定一个必须完成的指标，说“我每周必须在这几个平台上说出 X 句妙语”。我们看到的 traction 多得多的情况，反而是在主要的 Notion 账号稍微克制一点、等到真有有价值的话要说的时候才说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Any last closing thoughts before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。在进入超刺激的快问快答之前，还有什么收尾的想法吗？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Closing thoughts. No, this was a wonderful conversation. Thank you so much for letting me share. Truly, I also want to make sure I'm giving a lot of credit away from all the people that I mentioned throughout. It was all just a major team effort and I've gotten very, very lucky to work with the best people.
turns.zh: 收尾想法。没有，这是一场很棒的对话。非常感谢你让我分享。真的，我也想确保把很多 credit 给到我全程提到的所有人。那全都是一次重大的团队努力，而我能和最好的人共事，是非常、非常幸运的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We'll try to link to all of the people you mentioned in our show notes. We try to do that every time. So it'll be a long show notes. And we're not done yet. We've reached our very exciting lightning round. I am going to ask you six questions real quick. Whatever comes to mind, we'll go through it pretty fast. That sound good?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会在节目笔记里尽量链到所有你提到的人。我们每次都尽量这么做。所以这会是一份很长的节目笔记。而且我们还没完。我们到了超刺激的快问快答环节。我要很快问你六个问题。想到什么说什么，我们过得很快。可以吧？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. We'll see how it goes.
turns.zh: 好。看情况吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's go. No pressure. What are two to three books that you recommend most, that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。别紧张。你最推荐、你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Obviously Awesome by April Dunford. If you're looking to position your company, I don't know if you've read it, but it is a step-by-step guide. It's like 100 pages long.
turns.zh: 那当然是 April Dunford 的《Obviously Awesome》。如果你想给公司做定位，我不知道你读没读，但它是一本一步步的指南。大概 100 页。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've read it. She's done a guest post on my newsletter. She's been on the podcast. So all over it.
turns.zh: 我读过。她在我 newsletter 上写过客座文章。她也上过这档播客。所以很熟。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Oh, fantastic. She's incredible. Yes. Oh gosh. I'm going to have a hard time coming up with two other books that have had that sizable of an impact.
turns.zh: 噢，太棒了。她太厉害了。对。噢天，要我再想出两本影响有这么大的书，我有点难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We can keep it to one too. It's all good.
turns.zh: 一本也行。没关系的。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Can we keep it to one?
turns.zh: 我们能就保留一本吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. Just the one. All you need. What's a favorite other podcast that you listen to other than the one you're on currently?
turns.zh: 对。就一本。你需要的就这些。除了你现在上的这档，你还有哪档特别喜欢的播客在听？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I mean, I love your podcast.
turns.zh: 我是说，我很喜欢你的播客。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Harry Stubbings never ceases to amaze me. We've gone on at Notion a couple times and I just really appreciate his approach to mining a lot of incredible information and unexpected stuff.
turns.zh: Harry Stubbings 总是让我惊叹。我们在 Notion 上合作过几次，而我真的很欣赏他那种挖出大量不可思议、出人意料的信息的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Harry Stubbings is the godfather of this podcast because I did his podcast and at the end of it privately he's like, "Lenny, you need to do a podcast, you idiot. Why are you not doing a podcast?" And that got me over the hump and look at us now. So yeah, huge shout out to Harry.
turns.zh: Harry Stubbings 是这档播客的教父，因为我上了他的播客，结束后私下里他说“Lenny，你该做播客的，你这傻子。你为什么不做播客？”而那让我跨过了那个坎，看看我们现在。所以，对，给 Harry 一个大大的致敬。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I love all of these connections that exists. That's wonderful.
turns.zh: 我喜欢所有存在的这些连接。太妙了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Next question. Favorite recent movie or TV show that you've loved?
turns.zh: 对。下一个问题。你最近喜欢的一部电影或剧集？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Oh gosh. Recent. I went to go see Tar, which I know is going to be not everybody's cup of tea, but it was just incredible to watch this performance from Kate Blanchett. She learned German. She learned how to be a credible conductor of a major symphony orchestra. If you want to see a bravura performance, that's the one to see. And then recent television show I'm watching Fleischman is in Trouble. I love the book and I just think that the detail and texture of that show is super well done.
turns.zh: 噢天。最近的。我去看了《Tár》，我知道那不会合每个人的口味，但看 Kate Blanchett 的那场表演真的太不可思议了。她学了德语。她学会了怎么像一个靠谱的大交响乐团指挥。如果你想看一场炫技般的表演，那就是要看的那部。然后最近的剧集，我在看《Fleischman Is in Trouble》。我喜欢那本书，而我觉得那部剧的细节和质感做得特别好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. My wife and I have been watching that and it's awesome. Last episode was less exciting, so I'm curious where it all goes, but I'm watching.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我和我太太一直在看，确实很棒。上一集没那么精彩，所以我很好奇后面怎么发展，但我还在追。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Agreeing. But every time Claire Danes is on screen, I'm riveted. Yeah.
turns.zh: 同意。但每次 Claire Danes 出现在屏幕上，我就被吸引住了。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite interview question that you like to ask folks, either when you're interviewing at a place, hiring, anything that comes to mind.
turns.zh: 你最喜欢问人的一个面试问题——不管是你去某地面试、还是招人，任何能想到的。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. The one thing that was really helpful, because we used to do this thing at First Round Review where we would explore topics and be like, how do we get to a topics that's going to be unique or new knowledge or whatever it was. And it was, what is one thing that you think that led to your success that nobody else in your peer set has done? What was something that you did on a lark or that you were like, this is a big bet, or this isn't probably going to work, or it's a mistake that it even turned out this way, but it ended up being great. What is that one thing that was unusually conceived that you want to share with people?
turns.zh: 对。有一件事真的很有帮助，因为我们以前在 First Round Review 会做这种事：我们会去探索话题，然后想“我们怎么才能碰到一个独特、或是新知识的主题”之类的。而它就是：你觉得有什么一件事，促成了你的成功，而你的同侪里没人做过？什么是你一时兴起做的，或者你当时想“这是个大的赌注”、或者“这大概不会成”、或者“会搞成这样本身就算个错误”，但最后却变得特别好？那个构思不寻常、你想分享给别人的事，是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that question. I almost want to answer it, but let's move on. What are five SaaS products that you use or have used other than notion that you found to be really good other than maybe Slack, which everyone always mentions.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个问题。我差点就想回答了，但咱们继续。除了 Notion、也许还有大家总提到的 Slack，你用过、觉得真的好的五个 SaaS 产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I mean, I'm in love with Notion. The other thing, the other great love of my life right now is Arc, The Browser Company.
turns.zh: 我是说，我深爱 Notion。另一件、我现在生命中的另一大爱，是 Arc，就是 The Browser Company 那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God, I love Arc. I just switched to it. I love it.
turns.zh: 我的天，我爱 Arc。我刚换过去。我爱死它了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. It was something that I tried and within an hour I've made it my default browser and I just think it's beautiful and delightful in one of those intangible ways that a lot of these products are
turns.zh: 对。那是我试了一下、一小时内就把它设成了默认浏览器，而我觉得它就是以一种很多这类产品都有的、那种说不清道不明的美和愉悦感，让人喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same. Yes. Cool. Oh, there's more. Yeah.
turns.zh: 一样。对。酷。噢，还有更多。对。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I already talked about Figma. I love Figma. I actually use it in my day to day life, which is one of the best parts of it is that folks who are not necessarily designers or highly technical can also get a lot out of it. Superhuman. Couldn't live my life without Superhuman. Whenever I have to go back into Gmail to set an autoresponder or whatever, I'm like, ugh, my eyes. So couldn't live without that. Gosh, I'm on sabbatical, so I don't know how many other SaaS products I'm actually using day to day so I'm going to keep it at three.
turns.zh: 我已经聊过 Figma 了。我爱 Figma。我其实在日常里就用它，而它最棒的一点之一就是，不一定是非设计师或特别技术的人，也能从它身上得到很多。Superhuman。没有 Superhuman 我活不下去。每当我得回到 Gmail 去设个自动回复什么的，我就想“唉，我的眼”。所以没它我真活不了。天，我在休假，所以我不知道自己日常到底还在用多少别的 SaaS 产品，那我就说到三个为止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Yeah. Use less SaaS products during your sabbatical. It's a good philosophy.
turns.zh: 行。对。休假期间少用点 SaaS 产品。是个好哲学。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Yeah. I don't know if that was your experience, but just is. Oh, the other one I'll shout out, even though this is like a sneaky Notion plug is Kron. So if anybody isn't using the Kron calendar, which is now part of Notion as some folks might know, it is in fact the best calendar product on the market.
turns.zh: 对。不知道你是不是这种体验，但反正我是。噢，另一个我要喊出来的，虽然这像是偷偷给 Notion 打广告，是 Kron。所以如果有人还没用 Kron 日历——就像有些人可能知道，它现在已经是 Notion 的一部分了——它事实上是市面上最好的日历产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sneaky, sneaky. Last question. What's a favorite read or course or just anything you'd recommend for people to level up their community building skills to build a community, run a community? What would you point people to?
turns.zh: 偷偷的，偷偷的。最后一个问题。有没有哪本书、哪门课、或者任何东西，你会推荐给想提升建社区、运营社区本事的人？你会指人们去看什么？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: I'm not aware of any courses that are necessarily offered. Ben Lang has done a number of AMAs or interviews, so if you want to just Google Ben Lang and the word community or Notion, you're going to find just a lot of incredible insight. And his experience has been, I think ... In terms of community people operating in tech, Ben is top level, so find whatever he's said.
turns.zh: 我不知道有什么一定在开的课。Ben Lang 做过好几次 AMA 或采访，所以如果你想，就 Google 一下 Ben Lang 加上“社区”或“Notion”，你会找到大量不可思议的洞见。而他的经验，我觉得……在科技圈做社区的人里，Ben 是顶级，所以去找他说的任何东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We will find it. We will link to it. Camille, I just met you an hour ago, but I feel like I've known you forever. This was amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会找到的。我们会链过去。卡米尔，我一小时前才认识你，但感觉就像认识你一辈子了。这太精彩了。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Likewise. Thank you.
turns.zh: 彼此彼此。谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you so much for making time for this. Two last questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more? You're on sabbatical now, and so maybe share what you're thinking about next and what you could be ... I don't know. And I guess this is the second question. How can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 非常感谢你抽时间做这期。最后两个问题。如果人们想联系你、了解更多，能在哪里线上找到你？你现在在休假，所以也许分享一下你接下来在想什么、你可能……我不知道。然后我想这算第二个问题。听众怎么才能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Thank you for that. You can find me on Twitter. I'm just @CamilleRicketts. Super straightforward. Still sticking with it. And in terms of where I'm at in my life, I'm just interested in meeting as many fascinating new people and learning about things as possible. I've started going to these Founders You Should Know events for anybody who's interested about FYSK, and just meeting as many cool people who are building just incredible concepts. It's inspiring every time, and I just want my whole life to look like that. So get in touch if you're building something and think I could be helpful.
turns.zh: 谢谢你说这个。你可以在 Twitter 上找到我。就是 @CamilleRicketts。特别直接。还在坚持用。至于我的人生现在处于什么状态，我就是想尽可能多地认识有趣的新人、了解各种事。我开始去参加那些“Founders You Should Know”的活动，对任何对 FYSK 感兴趣的人——就是去认识尽可能多那些在打造不可思议概念的酷人。每次都让人受启发，而我就想让我整个人生都变成那个样子。所以如果你在打造什么东西、觉得我也许能帮上忙，请联系我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Camille, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。卡米尔，非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Camille Ricketts
turns.en: Thank you so much. This was wonderful.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。这太美好了。

turns.zh: 非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这期有价值，可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify，或者你最喜欢的播客 app 上订阅本节目。另外，请考虑给我们打个分或留个评论，因为这真的能帮到其他听众找到这档播客。你可以在 lennyspodcast.com 找到所有往期节目、或了解更多关于本节目。下期见。
